div.head: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
DEFEAT OF THE CONSERVATIVE GOVERNMENT. -- Tariff "Reform" Not Wanted.

There wo a large attendance and consider:Ode excite- meet prevailed at the meeting of the Wsrrington Parliamentary Debating Society ne Tuesday evening when the et:l.l.iog debate and dirk'on on the tariff " reform" resolution introduced by the Foreign Seer.. • tary (Mr. W. Furman, took place. Government and Opposition mustered in much stronger force than usual and the ape.hea were freely punctuated with ch.ra and interruptions which indicated a been interest in the subjto, of controversy. The result of the di•ittion caused great jubilation in the Liberal ranks, the Government being defeated hy sea. votes . •
reformers

The l'itrol DENT Or VI a Itc., Rl' or At:R.1.71.2E7er (Mr. C. ['Boston) said tn.!! return) far transcended in importance the Constitutional question, for the future of our workingmen and the late of tbe Empire depended upon it. It had made e wonderful advance it. public confidence, but there .as still a great deal of timidity. On this question the political parties bad changed places, the Conservatives being the party of prop.ess and the Liberals the party of conser•atism. (Laughter. • The Liberal party said all was well, because our trade returns showed an increase, bat they bed to admit that there were 13,000,000 people in thin country on the verge of hunger and tens of thousands who could lcurcely get the bare necessities of life. It might be said that provittions were cheap, but what was the use of cheap provisions without the means to buy them ? Under our preseut system we were treating foreign nations better than our own kith and kin. The Conservatise. did not pretend that tariff reform would find (cod for all the htingry and work for all the unemployed, but they maintained that it would reduce unemployment to a minimum. Ton speaker drew an analogy between Holland and Engl.& Both, he said, were Free Trade countries; both had unemployment, and both had to lace a grossing emigration. The people of England were going in large somber. to America and other protected coontriem, and the Dutch people were crossing the frostier to find employment in highly protected Germany. Under Protection Germany bad not only made herself a great manufac• taring country but Mid increased her agricultara What the Government proposed to do wee to revise the food taxes, allow raw material to enter the country free cif duty, and piece a ten per cent, duty on mannfactured goods, which would bring iu a large amount of revenue. (Applause.) Mr. E. LLOYD ( I Ombigh Borghs, said the resolution wee to keeping with the policy of the Con- j. Government which was one of assertion with- out facts. He declined to follow the Protectionists is be-lauding foreign nations. Ile via• an Imperialist in the truest seem of the word, and he believed in his own country. If Ciern.any and other countries were so good, why cry so ranch for a big navy ? Why not let them come and make tin as happy as they were? (Lstighter.) The object of reciprocity was to vomiter-1 age home induatries ny the raising of home prices. The system, however, would not attain the object in view. It would not improve our relations with the Colonies, who had riot seriously asked for what the Conservatives proposed to give. What we wanted to do wise to put oorselves in such a position that we would be able to give to the Colonies and ell other nations the best that we could produce, at the most reasonable price. What was needed was not tariff reform, hut the removal of internal obstacles to our deriving the full benefit of Free Trade. It was said by the Co... Uses that we were lighting with our hand• tied, lie sdrnitted it— hilt not by foreign tariffs. The evil was within and not without. Monopoly of land, royalti., high rates and over-lapping of railways, trusts and syndicates were all , things that hampered the development •f our tradeand I caused much mine.. Why not ten land and royalties instead of the children's broad? Tariff Reform was a foolish anti selfish crusade ; it might he termed a " top . dog" policy. lo every progressive movement some- body nom bleed, but why constantly bleed the loot? The CoLONI I. rirr HET, RV Alderman Bennett, said that at this moment we were needing at the parting of the waya with reference to the. affairs of this country E M and of the mpire. ould that he had the t (II nmet coke and eloquence of or, Gladstone or Mr. Chamberlain and the lei.rn and opportunity ! Ile would make thin land ring with the imminence of the crisis end the great danger to which we were exposed. Instead of (bathe hail to answer the somewhat feeble arguments of the gentlemen on the other tide of the house. (Laughter., Ile bad had his olfactory nerves offended by the everlasting red herrings trotted out by the gentlemen who advocated Free Trade in lieu of better argument.. (Mr. dl kUM An “Didyou overseen redherring trot "and great laughter.) The Metaphor might he miled,bot the argument applied. They never got to close quarters with the question. They were Always met with q nestle. about. m wog royalties, nationalisation of railways and taxes on land. They might be interesting—be 11 WA agree to some extort with the Opposition on these points—but they had iabsolutely nothing tsheteser to do with the case. Prectically every civilixed country in the world had a tariff to defend its own indual Hen That applied not only to the old States hut to new and progreseive nations, as was evidenced by .lapen. Holland, which for a long time wars bulwark of the Free Trade party, Wll9 revising her tariff, and going more in the direction of Protection. Our own kith and kin in the Colonies were Protectionists to • man. (. Question.") The party opposite seemed to lie much devoted to the rule of • mejoritit, They profeased to be cosmopolitans and to look at matters from a world-wide stand-point. Let them take a poll of the human race on this question. He wondered whether they would then leiguided by the decieien of the mejority or whether they woold wants lowilisei Second Chamber, consoose of effete Cohdenites whos ideas were utterly and hopelessly behind the age,to endeavour to run counter to the feel- ing and intelligence of thecivilited world. (Laughter). Socialists would admit that thetrueobjrct of production canto produce for our own use in our own country. One ot the objects of tariff reform teas to make it easier for thepeople if thiscountry tosupply their own wants. He regarded with consternation and dismay the preaent position of affairs. During the Boer war sonic disloyal member, of the Irish party cheered the defeats of the British force.. He regarded them as traitors to the Empire. He thought their loyalty waa suspect,but when he saw membern of the British House of Commone and their representatives in Warrington viewing with ill.concealedi delight a policy the end of which meant the disruption of the Britiah Empire, he really doubted whether there wasi much to Adios° between those Irishmen who cheered British reverses end those gentlemen who were unpatriotic and lolind enough to cheer the arrangements which were now being made across the Atlantic. Ever since the first Colonial Conference, Colonial

statesmen had been begging and praying of us to enter into close- fiscal relations with the Empire. We flouted thero----even his i the speaker'e)own party, before Mr. Chamberlain .iwOlte to the significsnce of the post- thin, treated them with coldnees and without that Imperial imagination which ought to characterise all English stateemen. dot since Mr. Chamberlain began his agitation the Conservatives had realized the import- ance of meeting the Colonie* in the matter. The Liberals had, however, been returned again and again by the people of this country who, in the words of Carlyle, he sometimes thought were mostly fools. (Laughter.) While they had been gratifying their petty spleen against an institution which he admitted was an anachronism, and which the Conservatives were anxious to reform---(laughter)—the golden oppor- tunity had *hipped. For the first time in the history of the Imperial Conferences the question of preference was omittal from the agenda of the forth- coming Colonial conference. The Colonies were sick of having the door banged and bolted in their faces. They had listened to the charmer and were about to make !an agreement with the United States. If they did that, the daye of the British Empire as we knew it were limited and we might already write over the portals of oar Parliament " Mean, Mene, Yokel, Upharsin." Of course, the queetion did not appeal to gentlemen opposite, except as as a subject for ribald jeers and hollow laughter, hut the time would come when they would curse their fatnity. By a scheme of Imperial federation we would have been able to defy the world and instead of our going cep in bred to the United State., that country would have had to come to us. (Applause). Mr. M. IlOw serif IL., FallUohtb , dealt with the statement Imo week of the member for Wekefield that the 't downfall of the wire trade" was due to Free Trade. During the last ten years practically all the large wire firms in this town had almost doubled thei_L products. Our export trade in wire and manufactured sir ire goods had grown front 11,150,1.00 to E2t2oo,otiry.

Our manufacture:a bad not only .captured the mci in the home market but their export trade gone up by leaps and bounds. div.head: "ONE DOES NOT BECOME OLD AT TABLE '
div.p: "ONE DOES NOT BECOME OLD AT TABLE '

is a characteristic saying in Italy, which means tha ! to sit over a pleasant meal is one of the joys of life. But it is at the end that the sweets and tasty dishes come. Delightful in a well-made pudding or sweet of any kind. It should, however, be of rise from a dietetic standpoint. Quite against common sense would be to COOl.llllO food regardless of its actual value. The sensible home caterer appreciates the fact and uses Currants in plenty because, apart from being palatable, they are Nature's own design for an ideal sweet, full of nourishing grape sugar, the best of all nutrients. Without Currants there would be no Christmas Pudding and no Mince Piers. The little fruit in the very essence of the success of our very best coafections. Of late, Currant cookery has been developed to a considerable extent, to the delight of all who taste the attractive dishes. An enormous number of delightful preparations can be made from Currants, which, apart from their great intrinsic value, blend perfectly with the other ingmlients which help to corstitute the sweet imam."

div.head: CARTER & SON Bridge St. Warrington. PRACTICAL POULTRY FARMING.
div.p: CARTER & SON Bridge St. Warrington. PRACTICAL POULTRY FARMING.
(By Redcap.)
HOUSING.

As in the affairs of human life, so in the pooltry world, the question of housing is an important one. It is of no one purchasing vsluable stock if they are badly housed, for good results will never come. Far better for fowls to roost in trees than in broken-down and draughty ro.ding place. And egain, however aultatantially built the house may be—if erected in a damp place—this also is detrimental to euccessfol poultry farmitig. 'the all essential points are as follows ; Well-built, plenty of light, perfect reptile- , lion and kept dry. These are not sunny points to remember, hut so very important are they that you should omit none. Whether it is more economical to porch:lee a fowl-louse or to construct one must be decided by certain circum- stances. If you reside in a neighbourhood where timber is cheap, and easy of access, then it would be cheaper to construct one yourselt. Of course, lam presuming that you are handy with tools. It is some- what strange, but nearly all lovers of poultry are heady in this direction. Still further : if you intend poultry-farming oats rather extensive scale, and all things being convenient, a great saving would be effected by personally erecting the fowl-houses. If you adopt this course, don't Ire tempted to make the operations too cheap by using inferior and thin timber. Boards used for poultoy Lowe@ should not be less than in. in thickness, the stouter the better : and when complete give them a good coating of tar. These ere important items, and well worth your closest obeervat ion.

There lea wonderful variety of poultry biome now on the market. and generally .peaking I have nothing but praise to offer to the !Tinny manufacturers now entering for the poultry public. If any complaint lies • in the output of ' shoddy ' houses it is often the fault of the purchaser. Again I say, avoid cheapness. A poultry house may be scientifically built. : but if c,in- strutted of cheap timbers it is a useless appliance. and helps to non failure in the poultry yaid. V cc must excuse vie dwelling somewhat on this point, ht, it is necessary to do •v. I have Bees manva good- looking poultry house weather-beaten and twivted all shapes in a -few weeks time ; especially in bail weather. It is no use having a fancy wood-work ridging with a draught-hole in the side. In all poultry appliance catalogues you have the matter of choice between cheapness and quality. Choose the ' latter it will pay you in the end. I

Whether for field Use, backyard or surburhan run, there is no more useful eyelet]) of housing poultry than the above. The scratching shed house is what is known a. a house constructed with two separate , compartments under the one roof; one portion is used las roosting quarters the other is used by the stock during inclement weather. The scratching shed of course is quite open-fronted save for a covering of wire-netting. Sometime.. sliding glass window is used in very severe weather and the latter is an excellent plan. Often enough in winter time the weather may he intensely cold and yet the sun may shine; therefore, when the sun pl.', upon the glass front of the ecratching shed it very materially warms the place and adds as a consequence'i to the general comfort of the fowls. A very important point to watch— when fixing the house and shed is to have the floor higher than the ground outside, no as to promote dryness. The drier you keep the houses that touch utote will disease he prevented. The nest boxes eltould be placed inside the scratching shed end rt perch erected along the back portion; this as well as the perches in the roosting cotupartment should be round and ale.ut 2in. in diameter.

During the RUITILIIer months frequent liter-wishing of the interior of the houses is essentiAl, and the perches should Itedreesed with paraffin oil; the latter is a good insecticide and when well soaked in the perch sockets it destroys that miserable little enemy, the red-mite. Every niche and crevice where these pests are likely to inhabit should be observed and treated as above. The lime-washing should be done., early in the torw noon as possible, no that it may be thoroughly dry before roosting time. If the lime is put on while it is hot et) much better, for it will not only dry quicker but serve as a good disinfectant as well.

Every availdble egg from the heavy or Ariatie breeds should be set this month. As one writer lan said, There is no chicken like a March chicken." With this f heartily agree, for if you want pullet, for next winter's egg supply you must hatch in March. True it is that you may get them by hatching out next month. lint to get • stock .•apable of supplying • succession of eggs you cannot afford to lose time. This in one of the busiest months in the poulti y card. The young chicks need every attention. See they do not get starved end feed them well and often en long as they eat greedily and clear up every meal. Take every advantage of the weather and gist' them as much liberty as pormible. A little linseed meal a. bled to the soft food occertionally, will assist feathering. And a supply of cut green I bone will make them etronger and increase their growth more rapidly. A careful eye should be kept on the breeding pens. Give the stitch plenty of wholesome food but avoid condiments in any form. A little piece of sulphate of iron in the drinking water will help to tone them up. Constantly renew the ' drinking water and keep up the supply of Hint grit. and oyster shell. Green food is still scarce, but you have II very good substitute in turnips and mangolde; these iris not difficult to procure. Finn, of the stock seem absolutely seedy" take them from the hen and give them a coddiver oil and quinine capsule. Csually a few days' rest with such treatment will pot them tight Use every endeavour to ohmic a good supply of fertile eggs. Thom of you who took the hint, and are raising a few early ducklings have need to be watchful. Keep them growing so that they may feather quickly and so al.. I fatten more speedily, remembering that as well as putting on flesh they have feathers to grow. It is a sure sign in young ducks-1111d if they feather well they will fetten early. Ere they feather a second time they should be killed and marketed. I hope you find there monthly notes useful. One cannot look to far ahead in the poultry industry. especially
at this season of the year. It ie only by these friendly remind., that I hope to &insist you ill making your pursuit, profitable. I`lo4 IMPLE 1111nov1,1F.A.

A profitable way of making nee of broody liens is by setting them on a batch of eggs and then selling hen and chicks together. Of course this system le useful where a large number are kept and when • lot of the hens are broody at one time. About half • dozen should be eat at the same time so that full batch. could be made up one from the other. If you happen to have an incubator run tide during the same period when all the hens could be supplied with sufli- . cient chicks. By so doing you would effect a sale ,d the full half-doyen hens, having sufficient chicks to hand. Now this method is not only profitalde as an immediate turn-oser, but is also a good tnetli,d of disputing of the slurp). broodi.. For ordinary laying stock a reasonable price to fix would be. each for the chicks (l'2 in number) and 2s. (id. for the hen, total Ss. tkl. all done in three weeks.

I.ISI. NI,. It is quite likely that you may have some difficulty in finding a sale for so many near home. If following an advertisement in the " "Examiner " you have to dispatch by rail. A few hints on how to do so will be useful. Take an ordinary grocery box about 18 inches , long by 12 inches witle.tnake a partition, allowing one section to receive the hen. The other will be for the chicks. The portion allotted to the youngsters shmild have a piemt o Darrow cardboard put round in an oval shape, so as to prevent them getting into 'lie corners of the box and being starved. Each corner should then be packed with cotton wadding and alto the bottom of the chick's department. Leave sufficient airspace at the top of the partition and bore a few holes in each end of the box at the top. Thus you get a Y urrent of dr right through. Before , finally dispatching give both hen and chicken. a sub-, stantial meal, ann that they may withstand what might be aometintea an unduly long journey. After making the lid very secure, paste on the top of it a label of latge type : " Live chicks with great care and haste." Needless to sac that from a humane point of view their journey would be facilitated. You cannot blame railway officials for neglect if the package is insufficiently instructive.

Berliner Teak,lett " had an article protesting agaimit ! what it dencribes " the con•oriiiiin of the 'Mi. !British ithopoing neck' into a IVI•111,0 against German trade." "Great Britain," it says," must clearly tinder- !mend that we arc, her beet customer after her colonies and dependencies. We buy from England large rpiantit iee of goods which, with a little goodwill, could le supplanted hy Getman ' products. Germeny, if ehe desired, could call into exiatence a counter-movement aiming at the exclusion of British manufacture', We should only appro. euch a course in dose of extreme neecesity, hut people in bingland ehould weigh well whether it i• rielly ra good idea to work up a campaign againet Germ. goods, and whether, if Germany wero forced to resift toe counter- movement, great damage for the United Kingdom would not ens.. Manufacturing towns like Bradford, blancheater, and Iluddersfleld ahould certainly offer an energetic uppieition to • boycott of Gernsan goods, for they could scarcely like to lose Germany as a customer.

div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
" ELIJAH."

I note with interest and satisfaction that our friend" o the Primitive Meth.,list Church, legh-street, selected the " Elijah " for the main purpose of their special musical service. I am old-fashioned—l bad almost written heretical—enough to love Mendelssohn, which the modern superior musical person affects to deride and discount, if not to desp:se outright. In the monumental work under consideration for the moment Mendelsaohn has presented tine great Tishbirc prophet in two wonderfully-contrasted phases. of character. Heroic, confident, and triumphant in the former part,. ender the strain of persecution he eventually breaks down and falls into despair, but from that state is rescued by the divine vision of lloreh. How admirably , it is all worked out inn the music. Think of the famous aria—the "almost hysterial petulance" of which has been the fruitful theme of critics in past days—" It is enough " ; the prayer for the raising of the widow's BOP, and later, the ono at Carmel, "Lined God of Abraham"; the scathing sarcasm at the expense of the prophets of Baal ; the truly Eastern character, "Is not his word like a lire" ; and the unquestionably immoital "0 rest in die Lord"--as indispensable on certain solemn occasions as in very different circumstances is the Wedding March from the same composer's delightful "Midsummer night's Dream" music. lam glad to think that our local choir, are not likely to let the public forget Mendelsaohn. LENT.

Apropos Lenten services now proceeding, our English lent corresponds with the French cari,me and the Italian quaresima, both revived from the Latin quadragesima. With St. Jerome, St. Leo, St. Augustine, and most of the Early Fathers, Romaniats believe that the fast is of the Apostolic origin. It does indeed seem pretty certain that the sixty-ninth Apostolic Canon, the Council of Nice in 325. that of Laodicea in :;61, and the Fathers of the second and the third centuries speak of Lent as a usage generally observed in the Church. Originally in the Latin Charch it extended only over :SG days. In the fifth century four days were added in imitation of the Saviour's fast. The Greeka are to-if ay and have been through the centuries, most severe upon themselves in times of fast, and much more frequent in their fasts. The Council of Toledo in 631 gave orders that those " who break the fast without necessity shall eat no meat for the net of the year," and one meal a day prevailed in this country in Lent up to the year 12,N), In the meantime, each practices have been--well, modified somewhat. OUR BUILDING SOCIETIES.

The annual meetings of Warrington Building Societies last week suggested a note which might possibly be of service 'to some. I cordially agree that the institution in question is one of the most useful in the country to the middle-claes investor, as, no far as our own district is concerned, it certainly is one of the most well-managed and worthy of confidence. As an stied pointed out not long ago, societies thus registered under 'the' Building Societies Act of 1871 have to conform to certain rules in ilie conduct of their business and the presentation of their accounts, so that a perusal of their rules and their annual report and accounts should give a very good idea as to the position of any particular society, and whether it is ono with which business relations might be safely entertained. A building society has to be looked at from two points .of view. An investor's situ into find one which trill give him the best return upon his money conuneumrate with safety. Ho will want to satisfy himself that the business is economi- cally managed, and that the properties upon which the funds are lent are of sufficient value to cover the loans. A borrower, on the other band, will want to find a society which will lend him the money he requires at the cheapest rate and free :from onerous conditions. It does not matter much to him how the society is managed, provided he obtains what he requirev upon advantageous terms. Where one person as frequently happens, proposee to be both an Inventor and a borrower, he ham to satisfy himself as to Cho ell-round merits of a society, and there should lie no difficulty in doing this 10-day, whatever may have been the case some

years ago. Before investing money in the shares of a building society it is always desirable to examine tic accounts in order to see the position they reveal, and the manner in which those of the registered society are net out renders this comparatively easy. Those responsible for the conduct of our local societies fearlessly challenge this minute examination. I may well abide reaulta with equamity. One has the utmost confidence in commending these well-established institutions to the notice of all sections ,of the , interested public. SYSTEMATIC READING.

Last week's note an to the " false economy and unenlightened policy " of in any way reatricting " the opportunities of reading which are afforded to the townspeople of Warrington " set me wondering if we fully appreciate the advantage of the reading circles which the National llome-reading Union is ever ready to encourage and f, ster, and which llonrish so luxuriantly in various parts of the country. For the information of any readers who way need it, let me explain that there are four courses of reading, afford- ing opportunities for different classes of ire:Were, viz., the young people's course, which in recommended as suitable for !scholars, and ulnae who have recently left school ; the intraluctory course for working people, who have not much time and money at their disposal ; and the general emirs!" arid special course, for more advanced readers. As one local hon, secretary of my aolliatntance pots it, the young reader entering upon the arena of life is like a tourist travelling in a for country. He needs a .hart, a sign-post, or a guide to direct him. This is the function of the N.H.R.U. in literature. It further aims at providing !stimulus, promoting thought, and encouraging an expression of °Mtn.. These aims are accomplished through the reading circle. It is desired to enlist in the circles those connected with religious, educational, literary, and scientific institutions, labour unions, persons wishing to advance theintellectual and moral improve- ment of the nation, and all those who wish to enjoy mutual help through reading circles. I am afraid , that Warrington has not yet made the beet of its privileges and opportunities in this respect. Quiet and commonplace as it may appear to some, it seems to me it cannot be too often repeated that the love of reading is one of the most valuable gifts we can inherit, and when rightly used becomes one of the moot important factors in moulding the character and enlightening the mind, and also one of the sweetest pleasures in human life. It is indeed desirable to use this power to its greatest extent, and in order to attain this end the reading should be broad, comprising the beat of both ancient awl modern authors, and at the same time be aystematie. Most emphatically, to close the branch libraries in this borough would be a retrograde step. HOW ROYALTY MAY ECONOMISE.

The other day while travelling by L. A V. Railway, I was much amused by the conversation of a fellow- passenger, who, among many other things, said Then again, there's all this here extravagance in dress. I reckon we all have to help to pay for the King's clothes in a way of speaking, haven't we ? Very well, what a lot of brass could be saved i' that there item alone. Just afore th last King died I wor reading 'at he had a matter o' 30 suite o' clothes. Just think ! And, you know, they can't possibly ha' been worn, an' it ' seems a shame 'at they should be wasted. They take a pride in wearing ohl lace that's been handed down through their grandmothers, and even farther back nor that ; and for ought I know tit' coronation robes that's served afore has to be altered sons to make 'ern do again. Now then, what! gay is this bete If an old coronation robe 010 Ito used cseer again wi' a bit of altering an' contriving, why can't other clothes be . made to wear the Mime way. Them there thirty suits 'at I was telling on could be used up by this new King without fresh 'tins having to be bought till they were done. I don't mean that they'd lit straight off, I dare nay the breeches might happen be a bit to big ; but they could be made to lit, an' there's one 'ad be fain enough o' th' job. Well, I'm gerrin' off here too so I'll bid you good day, but you just think o'er what I've said, an I think you'll agree Wl' me."

div.head: VILLAGE ENTERTAINMENT.
div.p: THE VILLAGE ENTERTAINMENT.
A QUICK ROAD TO FAME.

The impresinon that villdge performers—and in many instances the artiste, of the towns—are some- what :ikin to the conceited ISlalvolio in Shakespeare's "Twelfth Night" is for most people unexplainable. Ilot it !maim obvious explanation at the back of it. And in this column I propose to enlighten—though newspaper men might say deceive—thone who are in the dark an to the rens.r, for such affectation. I cannot blame' , them, for it in all the fault of the junior reporter, and the proof of this may be found in what I am about to relate.

When entering anewspaper office the aspiring junior is not trusted with affairs which have national migni- licence, but with such uniinportant yet necessary events as villagp concrete and entertainments and he is told with considerable emphasis that his account of such occurrences must not occupy many lines and if at the phrases which he pens should embody all the enthusiastic praise which his limited vocabulary permits. Now for you to get an adeqiiate idea of how the world of words moves, it is imperative that you should carry your mind to an unthly reporter's room of about D) feet square, with a low desk, bestrewn with innumerable papers, facing a diminutive window on one side, with a well laden shelf of books opposite, and in the middle a spacious table at which the chief reporter is neated strenuously engaged in turning out "copy" for the hungry com- positors who ore continually deploring the circum- stance that his nimble pen cannot travel more speedily if the already horrible caligraphy in to retain its legibility. The aforesaid low desk has room sufficient to serve the legitimate purposes of three normally sized individuals, baton the ocraaion 1 urn describing only one youth happens to be present. Ile is a dark haired, pale complexioned and neatly dreseed seven- teen year old tyro and in front of him is a freely pencilled pink programme of a "aketch" conceived by the village poet, who celebrated his achievement by offering alcoholic drinks to teetotal ladieS who were to take part in his production. The ekeich was pro- duced last night and the junior is writing his account. lie is puzzled. Ile has nearly got to Me end of his fourth slip et copy-paper and needs only to add a praiseworthy remark ti the name of a maiden. Up to now he has had a tremendous battle with words, being, I suppose, entirely oblivious of Dieraeli's and eve.ybody else's sensible observation that ideas are the realities and words express them. He believes in stringing words together, probably from the fact that he is young. Ile is an "entity . with a mind of my own," an he said : when he applied for Ilia berth" but can when the 1 Editor tio desires, exercise the virtue of docility." het : me see how he is progressing with his M.S.S. He haa designated Miss Stodge Trent as " a chartning unobtrusive lady who took the delicate part of wooer of the Prince.. ;" Miss Susie Crawahavr as the "dignified though gracious l'rinoess ;"" the play could not have proceeded smoothly if Miss Florence: Barrett had not paid special attention to her deport- ment ;" Miss Esther 'I ennant an " creditable ;" Miss Fanny cook as " splendid ;" Miss Eileen Kenyon an ".admirable," and no on. But he is now in a de•ilor- able fix for he cannot see any spiritualised form hovering around him with suggestions. He is looking round at the chief ; but the chief does not notice him —he is far too busy. For the fourth time he looks and then ventureathus :
Excuse no, Mr. Tinker, but I want a word for Miss May Andrew." . . . .

Try%iplendior" readily responds the man at the table, for he known how to do it. " Got that—won't do." "Try 'a charming lady' then.'' " Got that too'" "Got creditable ?“ " Yee." " Magnificent ?" " No, but that won't do, for she did not bate to do imuch."
"Whether she had murh or little to do is neither tn 7 fault nor yours, so midi it M and he oln‘rp nhout it !' the chief remarked hastily.
Like the good hoy he is he deem as ho in hidden, outs the M.H.S. into a small wooden cop, hears it go op the pneumatic tube, and heaves a sigh of otherwise inexpres.ible relief.
Since the above;ns rjtteia friend of mine has (crannied the following interesting correspondence on the understanding that I did not divulge his name.
FROM MI-S ANNIEW TO lIER OUST MARIA. Saturdk- evening,

Dear Auntie, oi Thanks for the lovely costume you sent ale this morning. It fits me handwainely. It wan a fine eighteen-year-old birthiley !gement. I told you a few days ago that I had 'wen naked t•i take Cousin Polly'e part in the entertainment at one pariah tea party. At first I was in an metal quandary, for I had never read the piece, never mind acted it ; and the other girls hail lieen practiaing twice weekly for three months. But I must have done well, for the "Courier " says I was " magnificent." Auntie, you know how modest lam, sot shall not wear the nieeenatuine you nest me to-morrow, for all the boys will be admiring me, and the girls will think I am vain. With legit love, your affectionate Niece, MAY.
IKtIER I Roll RISS TRENT TO MISS lENNkyI. Saturday murning.
I)ear Susie,

So sorry you are away, but I hope you are enjoying your holiday.. I see that the " Courier," with their usual ability for prancing merit when they Bee it, have written a good notice of our efforts. I send you by this post a copy of the paper for fear pm have not already warn one. I don't want to be egotictical, but you will observe dial it says more about me than it dors o you who were cn the stage far longer than I. Fancy just saying " creditable" about you when you were the centre of the whole affair. What makes it worse is that the paper has called Miss Andrew" magnificent " and site wee only on the platform for half a minute arranging the table. I expect she knew the reporter !—Au rerun?, MADGE.

div.head: WOOL TRADE.-1901-1910. EXTRAORDINARY INCREASE OF EXPORTS.
div.p: WOOL TRADE.-1901-1910. EXTRAORDINARY INCREASE OF EXPORTS.

The Woollen industry is one of the largest in the country, and the index on diagram indicates growth in millions. During the last decade it has made as much, or more, progress in proportion to its size as any of our industries. The exports of manu- factured woollen goods, which include yarns, have risen from twenty-one millions to thirty- seven millions,and the imports have dropped from eleven millions to eight and a half, showing together a trade gain of 1:13,924,622. No doubt part of this increase in the exports is due to higher prices of wool during the last two years,but after making the necessary deduction for this the growth has been almost phenomenal. The drop in the imports of two and a half million is also striking, and what is most
RY MR. C. E. PARKER.-NO. 7.

significant is that this drop is almost entirely in the most highly manufactured goods. Comparing this with the previous decade a striking trade recovery and advance is evi- dent. The fig,ires for 1891-1900 were : exports decrease £840,690; imports increase £331,975. Trade loss £1,172,665. The Wool Tables in the" Yorkshire Observer' show that the consumption of imported wool has risen from 150 million pounds weight in 1864, to 360 millions in 1894, and to 506 millions in 1910. That is that while in thirty years the increase was 105 millions, in the last six years the increase has been 144 millions.
No country in the world can in any way approach our record advance in woollen manufacture during the last decade.

The home team to a man pleyed a sterling game, but the •isitori were quite below form, Laves being by far the beat man on the Widnes side. The Hornets soon opened the scoring, Weet taking a wide pee from Banter in glorious style and running over at the corner after only • few minute.' play. Joni,, failed at goal. Shortly before the interval Jones wa• obstructed in the Widnes quarter, and from the free kick he landed • capital goal. Interval 1100re—i10Chditi• Hornets 5 points, Widows oil. The Hornets attacked strongly in the second half, but missed one or two good openings through over-eagerness. Right on time Jones received e pass from Schofield and dashed over with ate,, which he failed to improve. Reaelt—Rochdale Hornets 1 goal and 2 tries (9 points), Widnes nil. ST. HELENS UNFORTUNATE AT HOME. . .

Although they never at any period of the game played like a Cup-winning team, Leeds managed to pull through in their Cup-tie at St. Helens. About 9,000 spectators witnessed the match on the Enowsloy-rond !ground, and the gate receipts amounted to £l9B. The 111-fortune which doggol St. Hel.ns all through Cannot but have bad some influence upon the result. Three of their best players—the line. C. hi. Chaves., Harrison, and Trenwith—wereall incapacitated through injury, end to add to their misfortunes they had one of their half back; Greenwood, off the field for three portend the plan. St. Helene won the tom, and, playing with a .tiff breeze behind them, did nearly all the attacking forth. first half.hour of the game. Their forwards hustled the Leeds men to considerable purpose in the initial

etagee, but the try with which they took tbe lead after eix minute.' Miry wee very much- in the nature of a gift. Kelly had put in a big kick, and en the ball rolled over the line It ehould without difficulty have been made dead by Evans. The Welehnuto, however, missed the ball entirely, and in no doing presented Kelly with a simple try. Thiel wen followed a few minutes later by enother try credited to F.B.rton, who, after a round of muting, went o.er et the corner, deenite the gallant attempt, which Barron and Jarman made to tackle him. .

Then Leeds were able to rush s acrommage near the home line, end Topham end Whitaker dribbled over, With the remit that the latter eoored •try which Young converted. This lucerne Wee immediately followed by another, In which Jarman scored an unconverted try at the corner after peeving between Evan. and Oliver. Half-time :—Leeds, 1 goal 2 tries (8 point.), St. Helens 2 tries (6 points). It wart not until after having Iwon el roost constantly on the attack for twenty minutes that Leed• strengthened their position with another try, which , was well pawed at the corner by Oliver, who received A pees widely thrown out by Brookeby. Young failed at Igoe!, but a little later the Leeds full back was deeper- ately near with a drop kick which he made. Except for I two apasmodic and unprofitable excursion. into the eisitore' half. St. Helens had to be content to play the strict defensive game, nod that they accomplished very Well considering the disadvantage ender which they labonred. Result ,—Leerle I goal g tries (11 points), St. Helens 2 tries /6 points).

div.head: Warrington Overwhelmed at Wigan
div.p: Warrington Overwhelmed at Wigan

The Cop-tie career of the Wirepullers was cot abort in decisive fashion at Wigan on Saturday, when the Colliers woes great game by 21 points to 2. Roth sides were as selected, and though there bait been Pk lot of rain in the morning the ground rolled out in fine con- dition. Sunshine broke out and greatly improved the condition., while the crowd swfirmed round the flee enclosure. Warrington had probably a couple of I thousand aupporters with them, and by the time for kicking off there W 0,4120,000 people nmernbled sod the receipts totalled ECM The teams and oillabils were : Wigan—Sharrock, buck; Leytham, Jenkin., Todd end Miller, three-quarter back.; Gleam and Thome., half backs ; Sealing. Ramada's, Williams, Sheik:rose, Whittaker, and Francis, forwards. Werrington—Tillei, back ; Unsworth, Dicken.on. Teylor, and Waywell, throe-quarter beck.; Brooks and Creevey, half back i; Thomas, Shows, Johnston, Skelhorn, Moreno, and Naylor, forward.. Referee. Mr W McCutcheon, Oldham. Touch judge., Messrs W Johnson, Rochdale, and F Ratcliffe, Swinton.

' —Wigan" opened in strong fashion, and contrary to expectations their forward. rushed the game to the Warrington quarter by sheer strength and pace. Tilley defended coolly, but the Wloners would not he denied end an early penalty against Werrineton ge ve J. Thome• the chance to kick en easy goal. Warrington immedi- ately responded with strong play, and a ruck cused Sharrock to miekick in his own quarter. There were hopee of equalising as Warrington pot poseession, and ()leave ran offside. a Thome. had a goal-shot right in front al the poets, and missed badly In his attempt to emulate the score of his nameeeke. This aeemed a bed omen for Warrington, and they fell beck before another daubing dribble by Sealing and Francis. Play settled near the Warrington line, and the ball wee quickly heeled out to °leave—in fact it did not seem to bare been properly scrummaged. The halve, threw wide to Todd who gsve Miller a beau- tiful pees which took hire over near the flag. l'oor tackling by Warrington allowed the scorer to travel behind the posts, and Thomas added another goal. It we., treat to see the plucky coy Warrington came tip to scretch., again. The forwards never gave way and

booting Wigan for poraossion, the Warrington eacks bed a tern. Brooks, Creevey, Taylor, end Waywell handled beautifully. Leytham and Jenkins seem com- pletely beaten and Way,.ll sprinted finely tot the line. Neer the corner he was hemmed in and tressed inside to Taylor, the latter being tackled by Ramedale a few inches from the line. The effort deserved etc., and it wee slight compensation only when Warrington were awarded another penalty, and Thomas kicked a capital goal. This proved to be only a tempomry rellv by War- rington and the borne team soon resumed the offensive be means of superior play. A short run and punt by I. Thomas gave Tilley en awkward movement. He fielded the ball pluckily, but wan grassed near the line by Sealing and Miller, and enetained en injury to the ribs which forced him to retire from the game. Taylor fell beck to the rear position, and the next minute Wigan took the opportunity to increase these more. Glasse threw a wide pew to Todd, who sprinted well before banding to Jenkins for the centre to force his way over near the corner. There wee no goal, and the Interval came directly after with Wigan leading by ten points to two. There waa little hope for Warrington on resuming against the breeze. Tilley attempted to meat., and bad hardly taken 1 eylor's place when Johnny Thome slipped over from a scrum near the line. Leytham kicked a neat goal. Tilley retired permanently end Taylor reetnned as full-back with Johnston on the wing and rnsworth centre. Play was practically confined to the Warrington half, and efter a dashing rim by Jenkins Leytham crossed nose the flag though Txylor made a gallant attempt to stop hint. The five Warrington forward, put forth great efforts and succeeded in driving Wigan acmes the border. Brooks, Creevey, and Dickin. son combined in a nice effort, but the centre wee tackled in trying to double through. Miller snapped up the ball and made fine, dodgy run into the Warring- ton half, Brooks grassing him when he looked lib* ecoring. Wigan forced their way to the line, and Leythem charged a Warrington kick dowu and scored his second try far nut. Thie completed the scoring. In fact, Warrington had more of the name during the lard quarter then at any time since the commenaemeat, Brookes put in some agreesiye play, and Weywell was twice within inches of getting clear, but in the main Wigan were content to rent on their laurels. Final Wigan, three goals, five tries (2l points) ; Warrington one goal ;two points). BATLEY TOO STRONG FOR THE LINNETS.

Walker, Kennedy, and Padbury were next prominent with a dribble, and, following a good kick by Flanagan, the Batley end was invaded, In sortie loose play Anderson received a severe kiok on the bead, and he etired to receive medical attention. A smart kick by Flanagan gave his side an attacking position in the corner, and Kennedy, who charged down 13 evan's kick, cleverly picked upend forced his tray over with a try, Skew failing at goal. Although a men short, Batley fought well, end Drummond scored, try after the ball had been handled by Bevan and Loosemore. Lyons

div.head: iIRISH AFFAIRS. NOTES FOR IRISH READERS.
div.p: iIRISH AFFAIRS. NOTES FOR IRISH READERS.

Since the hopes of the Irish are inseparably associated with the early entry on the Statute Kook of the Veto Bill, it is probably correct to say that no utterance in the present flour, of Commons has occasioned more hope and encouragement to on than I the recent declaration of Mr. Asquith that the fire and paramount duty of the progremive parties is to , carry this Bill into law. The Government means bueinese. That simple and significant sentence with which Mr. Asquith closed a fine, highly levelled speech shows to the discerning mind that all the power., of intrigue, threats and the game of sham reform upon which the Unionists in their divided state depend, are to-day completely futile to stop the onward march of the people's cause. The catch cry of the Coercionist politicians unworthily uttered the other day by Mr. Balfour that the Government had introduced this piece of legislation, in a perturbed state, owing to their Parliamentary existence being at , the mercy of the Nationalists, came in for a crushing rammer when Mr. Asquith pointed out that the present , proposals had their origin in the policy of a Liberal I Government whose clear majority of 200 over all ports of the House, gave them absolute supremacy in the Commons. Nor was it less effective when hard fact was brought in to extinguish the myth of the Unionist contention that the Nationalists only cared for this epoch-making Bill becaMe it opened the way for Home Rule, In the veer ISB4, when the Liberal party had not taken up llome Rule, we find the Irish Nationalist members walking into the Lobby to sup- port Mr. Labouchere's resolution calling for a remedy of the malady of the House of Lords. Over and above the particular end peculiar quarrel which Ireland has had and still holds with this anachronism of our present State, her representatives at West- mineter have never missed an opportunity of hacking the democratic cause The stars in their courses, it has been said, are making towards an early settlement of the Irish question. That may be so or it may not be no, but certainly these greet debates in the new Parliament are making with increasing elearneey towards that much desired culmination. For what rational mind can bold the Unionist view, for example, that the vote of Nationalist members should be ruled out. That gives you the truly Gilbertian position of refusing the Irish members a vote in the Imperial Parliament and in the same breath denying them an Irish l'arliament ! The limit of the ludicrous is reached surely at that point, and the dispensations of nature most hem left some of our Unionists friends bereft both of imagination and accuse of humour or they would see to what an illogical sod farcical position they have been led.
THE NEED FOR ENLIGHTENMENT ON HOME RULE. •

The Horne Rule pr maganda goes on with arofiing force. By the long arm of coincidence. whilst Mr. Augustine Birrell was explaining what Home Rule meant to the Oxford undergreduates—those young gentlemen who by reason of high birth, wealth, and the other accidental forces of our strange social system are marked out for statesmen of to-morrow— Mr. John Dillon was addressing the metaphysical minds of the young Scot. of Aberdeen, mud Mr. .Joseph Devhn, at the special request of the Rev. Sylvester Horne, hIP.. was dealing with objections to Home Rule in the Vitra-Nonconformist atmos- phere of Whitefield's Tabernacle, London. At three important centres of thought, a question which we Irish have often heard treated as a jest, was the subject of serious discussion. The need for this enlightening campaign is not fully realised until it is understood how powerful and how numerous are the agencies which the Cnioniets oat of their weekly treasury continuously maintain. Take the newspapers of London. The greatest proportion, well-backed in finance, are bitterly anti-Irish and their screechings are echoed by imitators all over the provinces. Noth- ing is too mean in the crusade. If anyone be sceptical on that point, the elevation of a wrangle between husband and wife (an immemorial experience and coaval with human frailty) into • case of religious persecution, is conclusive evidence enough in all sanity. The utter dishonesty of this religious cry is clear from the evidence of protestants in Ireland today and the testimony of protestant historians of the Ireland of yesterday. Than the Catholic Church in Ireland, it is claimed by these historians, from Barrington to Lecky and Green, there is no finer record of any Church for t tleratiou. With- out wishing to writs one word that may make it harder for an Englishman- to understand, we may point out that the people whom faith was proscribed, the people who left their marble shrines for mountain sitars and who sacrificed their property and their lives in defence of their religion, these are the very people whom impartial critics my show no trace of bittern'ss towards the party which oppressed them. Politics apart, that single fact increases one's trust in human nature. And farther it suggests that the hit& are not no over- dosed with original sin as the hide.s calumny that Home Rule means Rome Rule necessarily implies. The Province of Quebec. which has Home Rule, is a Catholic State containing eight times as many Catholics as Protestants. The population represents the French, Irish and English race.. Yet where racial and religious differences appear in such striking relative proportions, in the Parliament of Quebec you have Catholic awl Protestant working for the common weal in perfect harmony. Not the loudest ant- Catholic platform-shaking orator would venture to say that in Quebec, where Protestants are in a greater minority than in Ireland, does Home Rule mean Rome Rule.

his best not to be merged into the mediocrities of Parliament. He has already made his maiden speech and his maiden blunder in the House of Commons. Towards -the end of Thursday's all-night sitting Mr. Smith intervened in support of an amendment for the allocation to local authorities Jot half the proceeds of the duties on land values, regardless of the fact that it was one of the Conserva- tive contentions only a short time ago that the land taxes would produce nothing. The Illember for Warrington's criticisms of the Government provoked ironical cries of "hear hear" from members"below the gangway."Mr 'Smith retorted with characteristic forcible- ness and made a reference to" impertinent insinuations" which drew a reproof from the Deputy Speaker. Eventually Mr. Smith had to " withdraw " more or less gracefully and plead "great provocation." Somehow or other, the Smith Brothers have a difficulty In speaking without being provocative, and apparently the House is disinclined to tolerate two of a kind!

There were several THE LICENSING points of interest aria- SESSIONS. ing out of the adjourned licensing sessions at Warrington yesterday. The Rector headed an influential deputation in support of a memorial dwelling upon the increasing drunkenness of Warrington and praying•the Bench to further reduce the number of licences in the borough. We are very pleased to find the leading churchman in War- rington lending his powerful aid to the cause of temperance in so direct and unequi- vocal a fashion, and only regret that the Warrington Bench hastens to do good at so slow a rate. Even with our increasing population there are still 192 licensed houses in the borough—a proportion of one to every 384 persons—and it is not -too much to ask that the proportion should be levelled down to one to 500 by refusing to grant 42 licences. Actually, only two were refused, though twelve had been objected to on the ground of redundancy. The Bench renewed the off- licence, 40, Kerfoot-street, the tenant of which recently pleaded guilty to supplying drink during prohibited hours on Sunday, and escaped with the absurdly light penalty of paying the costs. Once again the Chief Constable dutifully animadverted on the unfitness of this tenant to hold a licence, but the magistrates were hidebound by their own decision in the POlice Court and had to renew the licence or admit them- selves in the wrong. They renewed the licence, naturally I But the fact remains that they will suffer in public estimation so long as they fail to support their own Chief Constable in his efforts to enforce the licensing laws of the country with the-strictness which the nature of the trade makes imperative!

On Monday, Lord TARIFF REFORM Ampthill made an out- EMPIRE WRECKERS. rageous attack in the House of Lords upon Mr. Bryce, as British Ambassador to Wash- ington, because he lent his services to Canada, as it is the custom of the British Ambassador to do on such occasions, in its negotiations for the Reciprocity Agreement. Lord Midleton had the good sense to disclaim, for his party, this scandalous attack, which was sternly rebuked by Lord Morley. But the incident is a valuable reminder that Tariff Reformers, in their hostility to the Agree- ment, not because it is opposed to the best" interests either of Canada or the Empire, are ready to take up just the kind of attitude which lost the American Colonies to Great Britain.

There emerged from A KIND OF the debates on the REFORM. Parliament Bill this clear-cut impression. The Leaders of the Opposition are absolutely impenitent in regard to the Lords' obstruction , of progressive legislation and resistence of the popular will. Mr. Balfour declared him- self jr. favour of House of Lords reform, not because he admitted any fault in the House of Lords, but because he wanted a House which would show better on paper, and would, therefore, have a better chance of successful usurpation of -the privileges of the Commons. Lord Lansdowne's scheme for House of Lords' reform—the secret has been given away by Mr. Balfour—will be such as, in the words of Mr. F. E. Smith when describing last year a kind of reform that would be utterly useless, will "produce the same results as the present House ot Lords, but under less assailable forms."

div.head: VARRINCTON CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
div.p: VARRINCTON CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.

The half-yearly meeting of the society was held on Monday evening. Mr. Wadsworth presided and there were shout 150 member, present, its addition to the committee. The minutes of the merlons quarterly meeting were mimed end Messrs. Hall, Critchley sod Bennion, appointed scrutineer.. The committee's report (which was taken as read), Armed Rates for the half. year of £1 24,130 an increase of £14.603 over the corres- ponding period and R total of £241.946 for the 12 months,no Increase of £29,673 over NM The member- ship now stood at 10,695 a net increase of 817 on the year. The committee recommended that a dividend of 3s. 2d. in the El should be Fetid on all miles, including butchery, and the usual grants to the Education Fund and Thrift Fund according to role, placing the nelence to reserve. The nett profit after providing for all chorges. interest on charges and the Interim dividend was £10,77. The report and balance sheet after a few questions were passed. It vv.a decided to send two members as dale- eate, to the C.W.S. Quarterly meeting and Meagre. Witts, and Heyward were appointed. The Committee recommended an inereMlA of the annual subscription to the Warrington Infirmity from £l5 150.,—t0 £3l lot, elco new aubscriptions of £5 .se, each to Dr. Bernardo's and the Notional Children's Homes, and £2 2e., to the National Society for Preven- tion of Cruelty to Children. It was aloe moved and agreed to subscribe £5 ss. to St. Mary's Hospital for Women and Children at Manchester. The motion to re-open the question of the retiring allowance to the Into costlier was, on advice, ruled out of order by the obeirmon. The meeting cloned about 915 p.m.

Christian Endeavour and Saab! Trading. The Warrington District Christian Endeavour Cnion hare decided to hold an active out-door cam- paign on Sundays during the cooling summer against Sunday trading. They are ale° preparing a petition to present to the Watch Committee.

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
For a cold in the head Pliny prescribes a simple yet infallible remedy—three kisses on the mouth of a mule. We wonder what the result would be if the mule kissed first !

"Where else in tbe world," said the Home Secretary," is there such freedom as we have in London? Hare a man might live from year to year without a question being asked him u to who he was, and where he came from, what he did, or what he thought."

What is temperance beer? It appears, according to a judgment in a licensing case at the Borough Court on Tuesday, that even when the innocent teetotaller is quaffing his harmless ginger beer, he is actually indulg- ing—In a mild sense—in those spirituous liquors which he so much abhcrs. • _ •

The sum of £4 15s. 4d., made up of contri- btrtions fanging from one penny to 55., httt been raised in Warrington on behalf of the' ICoronation gift to the Queen, from bearers of the names" Mary," "May." and "Marion." The local effort was originated by the Mayoress, and the proceeds have been forwarded to the Lancashire fund

Lord Anglesey is endeavouring to restore his country seats to something like their former glory, and is buying privately some fine possessions in the way of furniture and pictures for their decoration. His most recent acquisition is a well- preserved fifteenth century Arras tapestry, for which he gave £6,600. The work illus- trates the story of the Seven Deadly Sins, and originally belonged to Cardinal Wolsey.

Alderman Tinnion denies with some warmth the imputation that the Corporation have " funked " the Sewerage question in Warrington, and we think there is some justification for his remarks. A scheme which will involve £150,000 cannot be hastily or lightly undertaken, and the longer the Committee can manage with the existing service, while at the same time preparing themselves for the inevitable and the more faithfully will they have fulfilled their obligations to the ratepayers.

Dr. Marsh, the successful co-defendant in the County Court sequeli to the recent Sunday motor car collision at Market Gate, is a well known international footballer. He played for Swinton in the palmy days of Valentine, and has taken part in many struggles on the Wilderspool ground. He has had the unique honour of playing for England and Scotland, having "qualified "as a Scot by being educated at Edinburgh University. On the day he did duty for Scotland he was first reserve for England. • _ •

Another triumph for British exports must be chronicled to-day, for we are exporting our time to France. But there will be no quarrel about it ; indeed, the Parisian will probably not observe the difference of his public clocks that are to be altered nearly ten minutes in order to bring them into line with Greenwich. The public clocks of Paris could stand a lot more change before anyone noticed that anything out of the way had happened. And no one will suffer for getting to work—and to bed—ten minutes earlier than before. • • • . . .

Somebody has !Caen suggesting that a ilkely source of Mr. Asquith's "Wait and See" was the memoirs of the Rev. Robert Hall. A correspondent on the other hand, thinks the Prime Minister had the expression trom "Dombey and Son." When the Dombey household are expectantly waiting the arrival home from their honeymoon tour of Mr. Dombey and Edith, Mr. Towlinson,' who "desires an opportunity of bringing down the spirits or the ladies to his own level," says, "Wait and see."

The power of the Crown to create peers, on the advice of the Prime Minister, where there is a dead-lock between the two Houses of Parliament, is the only remedy against persistent obstruction by the Lords. That it has seldom been used is due to the fact, as Bagehot points out in his "English Con- stitution," that, "just as the knowledge that his men can strike makes a master yield in order that they may not strike, so the know- ledge that their House could be swamped at the will of the King— ot the will of the people," has made the Lords usually give way when they have seen that the people were resolute.

Upwards of sixty members of the Orpheus Male Voice Choir, under their conductor. Mr. W. S. Nesbitt (who is also the conductor of the Warrington Male Voice Choir), gave a concert of sacred music for the prisoners at Strangeways on Sunday afternoon. Their audience numbered between 700 and 800. The singing was unusually good,even for this choir. The programme included "The word went forth" (Mendelssohn), Jenkins's har- monised version of Beethoven's "Hymn of Creation," "0 Thou whose beams" (Goss), "In Media Vita" (Max Bruch), " The Son of God goes forth to war" (Jenkins), and Sullivan's "The long day closes." Mr. Bennett North accompanied. • •

The sixteenth annual Council of the Evangelical Free Churches opened on Tues- day morning at Portsmouth. The Rev. Charles Brown, of London, was elected president, in succession to the Rev. Dr. Jowett. An address from the Council was presented to Dr. Jowett on the oceasion of his departure to America. In acknowledg- ment, Dr. Jowett alluded to the invitation to dine with the King, and said the King's last words to him were: "You go away with the goodwill of your King and Queen.' The Rev. Charles Brown, in his presidential address, dwelt upon the necessity of Free Churchmen getting more recognition from the State. He deprecated the tendency to filch away from the people the Sunday day of rest, and declared that the National Sunday League was exerting a most pernicious influence on the religious life of the nation. He spoke also in favour of more church unity. The Rev. Thomas Mitchell, of Southport, was nominated as president- elect. • •

The Council was more than a little bothered on Tuesday, by the details of a pro- jected improvement at the corner of River- road and Wilderspool Causeway. One plan was to cut a 60 feet roadway through from Chester-road to the Causeway, between the Vicarage and the crossings. This was strongly opposed by several members who expressed the opinion—an opinion we ' agree with—that a new road entering at such an angle on the Causeway would increase rather than lessen the dangers of the road at this point. Finally, the proposal was negatived by an amend ment, and referred back. The strongest conviction seemed to be in favour of demolishing the property on the south-west side of River-road, and thus relieving the congestion of traffic in a thoroughgoing

On Thursday evening at the General Wolfe Hotel, under the auspices of the Warrington Branch of the General Union of Braziers and Sheetmetal Worker., a supper and smoker were held on the occasion of the departure for Vancouver, 8.C., of Mr. 'l'. Whererer Scotsmen are gathered together there is joy iii the midst of them—an was evidenced by the gathering of the members and friends of the Warring- ton Caledonian Association in the Masonic Hall, Bold- street, on Thursday evening. Mr. J. L. Davenport presided, and the main feature of the evening was a lecture by the President, Mr. J. Fulton-Smith. During the evening Mrs. Margaret Booth and Mr. Westeott contributed Scotch songs, in their best , manner. Refreshments were served and were much enjoyed by those present. Mr. Smith took an his subject " James Hogg, the Ettrick Shepherd." Be said that Bing lived somewhere about DM years no and was reckoned among his compeers as the most active and meditative uneducated poet of his time. He did not have much schooling for at a very early age it was necessary for him to assist the family funds, which he did by acting as a shepherd. On the hillside he bad ample opportunity for contemplation which just suited his temperament. Surrounded be great hills and amidst beautiful fields—nature being his constant companion---lie allowed his imagination fall scope and olttmately became one of Scotlisnol's best ballad songsters. At that time his songs were very popular, attaining the great vogue which they merited. On the proposition of Mr. W. Murray, a' vote of thanks was accorded to the lecturer. Vote of thanks were alto moved to the artistes and ladies who had prepared the refreshments. and to Mr. Davenport for presiding, by Mr. J. jtlcltermid and Mr. Smith respectively. Academy-street Adult School. Mr. James Hall is an es t eclat favourite at the Acalemy-street Adult School, and on Sunday morn- ing lust he fully maintained his reputation). Taking for hie subject, the much debated question " Sacialient and Chrintianity " he expressed his view% explicitly, in plain, coherent language. Ile believnd in a religion basis for all vcial reform, religion being mile a binding, compelling, lifting force, as it were. to higher power; and much is the essence of all religions, sod in this Christianity and Socialism have Mention' relatiamehip. Christianity held up the Fatherhood of tind.and the brotherhod of man,ss their goal, example or ideal, and Christ Himself made it palpably clear in His parable of the (fool Samaritan. how best to serve God, which in just the ideal nod ambitions of the more intellectual class of Socialists. There are however such divergencies of opinion as to Christianity and Socialism, that he was not surprised that occasionally on one sideSocielista were looked upon as atheistic, and on the other the Church and Chapel adherents were designated " a group of hypocrites." S. cialiam means more than mere national ownership of production and mean, of exchange. It means the sense of relationship between man and man, and the sense of our duty individually to the whole con). num it• ; and it in here that Clirietianiry and Soci•liern have their common meeting ground. Thelast evntury was responsible for greet scientific discoveries, that have brought about the control of natural forces for the use of man, a g., steam and electricity. This has resulted in readier mean. of providing food, clothing and shelter far the human race. Unfortunately, avarice on one side and poverty on the other, have eerionaly impeded a Met dietribution of the benefits accruing; and it in this momentous question which Socialists are trying to tackle, and to which the Church is hound to give greater attention in the futute. 'Heald upon the principles of Jesus Christ. his (the speaker's) idea of S was quite convisteot with I, true Christunity, and in thst cane, there would be no , fear of it developing into a State-regulatsd machine, : but would offer facilities to all, by removing poverty and dealing with the resources of the country in a proper and he dilly manner. Sociallsm ought to provide a fit environment for what is best in human nature.

This is a notable year in the history of Chrint Church, Igtchford, Jr on July lfili he fiftieth anniversary of the consecration of the building will he ettlebraied. Christ Church was erected in memory I the late Thorn. Green*ll, of Wilderepool and Grappenhall, by his children. It it a small but graceful Gothic structure, n ith an ornamental tower of pleaaingdeaign—in fact it in generally considered to lie one of the prettiest churches in Warrington and ilistrict. It wan consecrated on July lllth, 18011, by hr. I.:reliant, then Bishop of Cheater, us a chapel-of- ease in the parish of Grappenhall. The following inscription, which modestly omit• all allusion to the founders, was placed on a braes plate in the church to commemorate the event
To the glory of God and in affectionate memory of the late Thoman tireenall, of Wilderapool and Grappenhall thin church was erected Anno Domini Mil.

iln his history of Latchford, Mr. W. 13eamont records I the fact that the mason. employed In building the steeple, of their own accord, sculptured on the two corbels of is south window portrait likenesses of General Garabaldi and his Lieutenant, Colouel Psed, two of the most popular heroes of the time who, we must suppose, were the sculpt w's favottritss , " l'ulesa however," comments Mr. Brownout " they I thought that they belonged to the Church Militant they made a mistake in placing them where they are." By an Order to Council of Mach 12th, 1800, Christ Church was made a parish and a separate district was assigned to it, containing a moderate area and a population St that time of 1031. Since then Latch- ford has grown considet ably and to-day the pariah has over 1,1100 inhabitants. The church, which contains some excellent modern glass. and is beautifully decorated, was enlarged by the addition of a transept and organ chamber is and further enlarged by the provision of a north aisle io 1902. The list of incumbents from the consecration of the church is as follows
184 A-1865 Rev. Richard Greenish ettrate-in-charge). 1865 - 1870 Rev. W. R. Burgess (111 Vicar). 1870-1878 Rev. T. W. Powell. 1878-1809 Rev. B. B. Prescott. 1890-1903 Rev. F. A. Screeton. _ _

1504 Rev. G. C. Briggs. The present vicar (Rev. G. C. Briggs, M.A.) in the son of the late Mr. Thomas Briggs and was born at Seedley, Lancashire, in 1872. He was educated at the Moravian School, Neu•ted, Germany, and afterward. at Sidney Sussex College, Cambridge. Be took the degree of B.A. in 1804 and M.A. in 1899. Be wee ordain. d deacon by the Bishop of Chester in Chester Cathedral in 1855 and priest in 1896. Mr. Briggs was assistant curate of St. Barnabas', Crewe, from 1895 to 1807. Next he held the curacy of St. John the Baptist, Chester, with charge of St. Barnabas' mission. He worked there from 1807 to 1904, under the direction of the Rev. Canon Cooper Scott, the mission which was his apecial sphere being situated in a very populous district. In January, 1004, Mr. Briggs was appointed by the Rev. Richard (treenail to the vicarage of Chriat Church, Latchford. It is a ; singular coincidence that Mr. Briggs was the ' immediate successor of the Rev. F. A. Sereeton at St. Barnaltes' mission as well as at Christ Church, Latchford The affection in which he was held by his flock at Chester was strikingly evidenced, when, on his departure for Latchford, they presented him with an illuminated address, a purse 01 gold, and a hand- some clock. Mr. liriggs was the President of the Chester Whist League,consisting of representatives of the various young rnen's inetitutes in the city, and he was the recipient of a pair of silver candlesticks as a token of regard from that organization. At Christ Church, Latchford, Mr. Briggs has proved himself a hard-working, sympathetic and pond priest, and the church is in a most healthy and progressive state. An important feature ofthe work in which Mr. Briggs takes • particularly keen interest is the parochial branch a the Church of England Men's Society,which has enlisted the help of a large and enthusiastic band of young men. Mr. 13rigge is convinced that there is a great future before this society which has for its main object. " (a), to band together men in a united effort to promote the glory of God, and the increase of His Kingdom; (Id, to promote and deepen the spiritual life among members soil associates ; (c) to promote opportunities for social intercourse armor; members and asocisteri." The church has over 400 communicants and there is a flourishing Sunday school of about :;50 children. Special services for children are conducted by laymen in the parish room every Sunday evenisg, Councillor Wilson being the superintendent. Other useful sections of the church's activities are the large Bible classes for men and women, superintended my Mr. J. LEirth and Mrs. Deacon respectively. The band of hope,conducted by Mr. J.J.Firth,is wonderfully well organized and in doing a splendid work, its member- ship being 1.50. Mr. Briggs is warm in his acknow- ledgement of the valuable help which he receives front the Sunday school teachers, district visitors and other lay workers, who devote themselves most ungiudgingly to the advancement of Church life in the parish. During the Mayoralty of Alderman Forshaw ;from 1908 to 1910) Mr. Briggs held the office of Mayor's chaplain, and the sermons which he preached on the occasion of the official visits of the Mayor and Corporation to the Parish Church were characterised Ity breadth of outlook and the proclaim- ing of a lofty ideal ill civic work.

The wcond of a serial of three lectures in connection with the New Church was delivered in the Masonic flail, Bold-street, on Wednesday evening, by the Rev. John Howard, of Bolton. 'raking for his subject," Is the Bible the Word of God ?" the letterer said that on the consideration and meditation of that question rested the whole fabric of religion, belief, for religions belief was based upon the sacred Scripturev. To the Christian it was the bedrock and foundation of him belief and, therefore, to take away the Bible was to shatter all the hopes and longings of men. Th.t night he was not there to prove the existence of God. That was an hypothesis slready accepted. Ile was there to Prove the 13 ypothesi• that the Bible wan the Word of God. There was a condition of unmet at the prewnt limo cawing men to engender a spirit of doubt and even disbelief, which wee perhaps due more to what : had been falsely called the researchea of the higher critic.. They need not he aorprised with the funk that an, manifest, when the doctrine. no called of the critics were proclaimed from the pulpit. The whole subject was involved in the question of inspire. tion and revelation. Though they were closely related : they were very different things. Vet they had often been confounded as synonymous. Inspiration wait breathing into; revelation wan an unveiling and uncovering. Therefore, among chriatiank inspiration meant the indication of God's thoughts and ideas to man and revelation meant the unveiling of the I tickle thought and the Di•ioe idea of man Thew was nothing in the fact of Jewish history or the prophesies to distinguish them from other human documents and men of intelligence had considered that evidence an] proof that the book was not the wisdom of God. That was a mistaken coLlClllgion, because the Ettnnan etandard was almost uppermost in men's thought and accord- ingly men pawed judgment as they did there. If the Word claimed tube Divine and the Divinity did not appear on the surface they could not reanonably say on that account that the claim was a (vine elle. Vet, that WAS What the critics were flaying of aacred booka. But if the Bible was the Word of God it must he like His works, contain infinite and more glorious truths Bum were to he found on the surface. Because wisdom was net to lie found on the surface by some was no more proof I at/tin/it ton wisdom contained in the Bible than the fact ' that the spiritual wan invisible was evidence agninst its reality, The Bible was not intended to teach natural ululate t religion was not an earthy science RINI nature coullll not create religion. div.head: FUNERAL OF ADMIRAL CURZON-:-lOWE.
div.p: FUNERAL OF ADMIRAL CURZON-:-lOWE.

The funeral of the Commander-in-Chief at Portsmouth, Admiral Sir A. Curzon-Howe, Was Cu imposing ceremony, accompanied by full naval honours. The first part of the funeral service was held in Portsmouth Dockyard and Church, and the body was afterwards taken to Highcliffe, near Bournemouth. The late Admiral had a distinguished career; joining the Navy at the age of thirteen, he became captain at 38, and later had commando' the China Station, and in succession the Channel, Atlantic, and Mediterranean Fleets.

Lord Crewe, the Secretary of State for India, is suffering from the effects of con- cussion of the brain, caused by a fall at an Official dinner party. The accident will necessarily incapacitate Lord Crewe from fulfilling his duties as Leader of the Govern. Orient in the House of Lords, and it may be • couple of monihs before he will be again able to appear there. Viscount Morley will for the time being act as Government Leader in the Upper House, and take temporary charge at the India Office.

DR. JOWETT'S FAREWELL Prior to his departure for New York, Dr. Jowett preached his farewell sermon al Carr's Lane, Birmingham, on Sunday last, ft a crowded congregation. It is 16 yeart ago that he was called to Carr's Lane If succeed Dr. Dale. Year after year his popu larity has grown, and his preaching attractee large congregations. Dr. Jowelt. who has held the office of President of the Fres Church Council and Chairman of the Co. teegational Union, has received many offers to leave Birmingham but declined them. Is accepting the offer to go to Fifth Aveom Church, New York ,it is the vast cpportunita for an evangeli,al ministry in America tba made such a powerful appeal to him.
