div.head: CHAPTER ON SUN-DIALS.
div.p: A CHAPTER ON SUN-DIALS.
A GENERAL HOMILY WITH A LOCAL TEXT.
It i 24 only the initiated few who know the quiet corner in Stanley Street where an old sun-dial lingers, and not many, we think have read its inscription:
VIRTUE Joie Pervious TIM E. The gift of Peter Wiest ,cloy to the publick of Stsuley Btreet, %lilies/toe. 1755.
It is a reminder that there was a day not long past when a sun-dial was a boon, and the name of its donor handed on like that of the patriarch who digged a well. . _

Of the Peter Winsta-trley who raised this stone pillar we reserve mention, reserving reference also for an indefinite period to the incident of its removal a short time ago and subsequent restoration. It will be enough for the present if we say that it formerly had the dignity of circular steps which the raising of the surface of the street has left underground.
The-Stanley-street sun-dial, with its terse motto, differs in no respect from the average time-teller of its period, and for that reason will serve us well as the text for a little homily.

div.head: CHARLES LAMB'S HOMILY ON SUN-DIALS.
div.p: CHARLES LAMB'S HOMILY ON SUN-DIALS.

The classic passage on. the sun-dial was written by Charles Lamb in his superb "Ella," and no writer on the subject since has been able to refrain the quoting of it? What an antique sir bad the now almost effaced sun-dials, with their moral inscriptions, seeming °revels with that time which they measured, and to take their revelations of its flight immediately from heaven, bolding corres- pondence with the fountain of light! How would the dark line steal imperceptibly on, watched by the eye of childhood, eager to detect is move- ment never retched, nice as an evanescent cloud, or the first step of sleep ' Ah ! yet doth beauty like a dial hand Steal from its figures, and no pace perceived ! What • dead thing is a clock, with its ponderous embowelmenta of lead and brass, ire pert or solemn dulness of communication compared with

A GLOBE SUN-DIAL DOUBLE CYLINDRICAL SUN-DIAL. Our illustrations are lent by Messrs. Barker and Son, 12, Clerkenwell-road, London, who are specialists in the art of dialling, and who make sun-dials and vanes of every kind. The dials illustrated are of ingenious and unusual designs.

the simple altar-like structure and silent heart- language of the old dial! It stood ea the garden god of Christian gardens. Why has it almost everywhere vanished? If it. business use be superseded by MOTO elaborate inventions, its moral uses, its beauty, might have pleaded for its continuance. It spoke of moderate labours, of pleasures not protracted after sunset, of temper- ance and good hours. It was the primitive clock, the horologe of the first world. Adam could scarce have missed it in Parsdiee. It was the measure appropriate for sweet plants and flowers to spring by ; for the birds to apportion their silver warbling@ by; for flocks to pasture and be led to fold by. The shepherd • carved it out quaintly in the sun, and, turning philosopher by the very oczapatiim, provided it with mottoes more touch- ing than tombstones.
Thal touches at once and for ever the poetry of the sun-dial. It will never need to be said again, . .
But som— e folks want to know the science even of a moss-covered ivy circled sun-dial and for their consolement something must be added. THE SCIENCE OF THE SUN-DIAL.
I am a shadow,

When the Arab plants his spear in the sand and guesses the " time o' day" from the length of its shadow he is following a plan which his fathers have used for long mil- leniums. The interpretation of the text in the book of Job "As the servant earnestly desireth the shadow " may be found any- where in Egypt to-day by those who watch the field labourers in their method of dis- covering how far the day has run and how far off the hour of rest.
So art thou ; I mark time ! Dalt thou? Other gems of brevity are Light rules me, The Shadow thee. And
Heaven is my guide, I cannot go Wrong.

It is a surprise to realize that this measuring of a shadow is the basis of all astronomical and geometrical science. The Egyptians were not long in discovering that they could learn also by the variations of the shadow the length of the year. The discovery that gave accuracy to the dial was that of the placing of the gnomen or rod that casts the shadowN To the Ancients it would come by experi- ment, but we can put the matter in clear and easy terms and readily make a perfect dial.
For him dark day, do not exiat— The brazen-faced old optimizt."

The gnomen must be placed parallel with the earth's axis. This means that a sun- dial must be made specially for the latitude in which it is to be placed. A dial that is correct in London would be useless in Scotland. In London its angle would be 511 degrees in Scotland 55. In Warrington it would be about 54. At what ever point !the dial is to be placed the rod or gnomen must point accurately to the Pole Star.
A Clock the time may wrongly tell, I, never, if the Sun shine well.

Having got a correctly placed gnomon it only remains to inscribe the hours. The amateur in dialling must be cautious here, for there are only four days in a year when he can correctly mark his dial. On every other day his watch, which tells Greenwich time, and his dial,lwhich tells Solar time, will differ. In November the sun will be a quarter of an hour too soon, in March he will be ten minutes slow. In April he will improve and in May begin to get fast. . -
Go about your businegi,

These things are not very familiar to us, but they used to be taught in every village school once upon a time, and "dialling" was so common a subject that any save a very dull youth could make a dial upon his cottage wall.

But the coming of public clocks and cheap I watches has changed all that, and the dials that linger in our churchyard are almost the only reminders of a day when in eur own country the" servant earnestly desired the shadow."

The gods confound the man who first found out Row to distinguish hours. Confound him too Who in this race set up • sundial To cut and hack my days on wretchedly Into small pieces. When I wan • boy, My stomach told me when 'twas proper time To go to dinner, when I bad ought to eat ; But nowadays, why even when I have, I can't fall to unless the sun gives leave. At first dial 'pillars were plain, but when taste began to improve good work was lavished upon them, and we have old examples with us which are beyond all parise for their stately grace and beauty. Then came the motto, also in the sixteenth century, and with it all that poetic taste and terse wit could express. . .
A sundial motto; must needs be brief; it must also be appropriate. Let Us see how well our rhyming ancestors could handle their mother tongue. The one we judge most perfect is at Stirling
The fact that the dial only records the bright hours has inspired many a motto, of which we may just give one example.
Let other tell of storms and showers, I'll only count your sunny home. A couplet which drew from Alison the lines " Serene be atands among the flowers, And only marks life's sunny hours ;
When clocks became common the wits could not resist the opportunity of a com- parison, and one old dial is made to sing,

There are some Latin mottoes, too, that deserve quotation. Sol me tot Umbra Regit (The Sue guides me, the shadow you). Lax et umbra viciesim eed simper minor (Light and Shadow by turns, but always Mm). Pereunt it Imputantur (They pass by and are reckoned). And which could be a neater stimulant than Haste ! oh haste ! thou sluggard haste ! The present Is already past. or the gruff
Another we copied not long ago is very good

Shadow and Sun—so, too, our lives are made, Yet think how great the sun how email the shade. And among the moralising verses perhaps a place may be spared for this. " Abuee me not, I do no ill : I stand to serve thee with good will. As careful then be sure thou be To serve thy God, as I nerve thee."

It is not to be wondered that the dial has inspired beautiful words. Nor need we wonder at the mingled sadness. The swiftness of time, the brevity of life, the lost regretted hours and the dark shadow at last when the sun rests behind the hill. All these are written upon the dial face for those who look with the heart as with the eye. "Light and shadow by turns but always love" is written upon a dial face. It is written also across the page of life. A.M.

div.head: SUN-DIAL IN HISTORY.
div.p: THE SUN-DIAL IN HISTORY.
J6llaMemmssa•.

Looking back there is much to linger upon in the old plan of time telling. Cleopatra's needle, so the arclueologists think, was probably a time-teller, white stones being placed on the ground as the hour-stones to which shadow pointed.

The first clear reference to a sun-dial belongs to a period in the eighth century B. C and occurs in the book of Isaiah ; "Behold I will bring again the shadow of the degrees I which is gone down in the sun-dial of Ahaz, ten degrees backward," but of the typo of which we have no sure knowledge. Greece first knew the scientific sun-dial in 1560 B.C. and it owed the introduction to I Aniximander of Miletus. The Romans copied, as in so many other things, and the first dial was fixed at Rome in 293 D.C. in the Icourt of one of the temples. Cicero refers to I the sun-dial he wished to put up at his villa, and when a raven struck the gnomen from his dial it was regarded as an omen of hisl I death.

Among the Romans there was a period when the dial became a universal fashion. They were placed on temples, houses and baths, and they later became the fashion as tomb stones. Of this custom one of their cynical poets said, that it was adopted as the only method by which they could induce posterity to read their epitaph. We cannot get back far enough to know , from whom Israel, Greece and Rome gained knowledge of the dial, but doubtless it was Ifrom that old home of Science, Chaldea. China has long known it and the dial is as familiar there as the clock is here, and in Japan pocket dials are carried as we carry watches.

The oldest English sun-dial is believed to be that at Newcastle Cross which dates to A.D. 670. Early as this date .say seem it is not impossible. In Norman England dials were placed upon public buildings as we now use clocks, and pillars were set in open spaces like the obelisks of Egy-t. The name "Seven Dials in London preserves the memory of the pillar which stood there at the junction of seven roads. In the sixteenth century the private dial came into fashion and gentle folks began to put them in their gardens, or, more unsel- fishly, to place them where the passer by might read the shadow. The kindness was not universally appreciated and there are some quaint old lines in which a poet voices the feeling of the man in the lane.

div.head: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT. i
div.p: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT. i
by Philip Snowden, NP. THE NEW TRADE UNION BILL

Parliament and public interest in politics are for the time being F o wholly absorbed in the House of Lords' controversy, that the question of the reversal of the decision in the Osborne case is for the moment in the background. But the matter is by no means being allowed to rest. The Parliamentary , Labour Party are keeping the question in mind, and are fully prepared to press it for- ward as soon as the first favourable moment comes. By the way of being prepared for the first opportunity, the Party last week introduced a Bill to deal with the matter. The Bill, of course, has no chance of being discussed -unless the Government should grant some special facilities for that purpose. It is not yet certain that such facilities will not be granted. Indeed, I think it may be assumed with confidence that either on this Bill of the Labour Party, or on some pro- posal which the Government themselves will bring forward,the whole question will come before the House of Commons as soon as the Veto Bill has been got out ofthe way. The Labour Party's Bill is a very simple Jae. It has only one operative clause. I had better give the text of that clause. It reads as follows:

"A Trade Union as defined by Section 16 of the Trade Union Act Amendment Act, 11876, may, notwithstanding any of the Iprovisions of the Trade Union Acts, 1871 and 1876, either acting by itself or in conjunction with any other Trade Union, association, or body, apply its funds for or towards the purpose of procuring the return and provid- ing for the maintenance of members of Parliament, or public or local authority, or of any other public body, and may do such other acts as may be necessary to further the interests of workmen by political action or otherwise."

The meaning of this clause is that political action shall be one of the legal functions of a trade union, and that it shall be lawful for a trade union to apply its funds for the pur- pose of promoting Labour candidatures for Parliament and for local bodies. In order to make the Labour Party as at present con- stituted a legal body, it is provided that a trade union shall be entitled to join with other trade unions, or with any association or body, for the common promotion of candi- dates. It will be noticed on a careful examination of the clause that, though it contains very few words, it embodies a great deal and covers a very wide range of powers. It gives trade unions legal powers, not only to pay members of Parliament, but to pay their representatives on local bodies also. Under the law as it has been interpreted by the House of Lords in the Osborne decision, a trade union cannot use any portion of its funds for municipal purposes, nor can its organisation he used to promote the return of Labour candidates to the Town Councils and other local bodies. But this Bill, if it became law, would give the 13owers which have been used very extensively in the past, and which have been used in the most innocent confidence that it was a perfectly lawful thing to do.

div.head: FREE CHOICE AFFORDED.
div.p: FREE CHOICE AFFORDED.

There is another aspect of this Bill I should I like to point out. Of course the clause itself says nothing about the politics of the candi- dates the trade unions may finance. It will not be necessary to give legality to a trade union candidate, that he should be a candi- date promoted under the constitution of the Labour Party. The Bill simply gives the legal power to a trade union to use its funds to promote Candidatures. The conditions of the candidature will be determined by the trade union. Under the Bill, these will be settled by the majority vote of the members. If the majority of the members of the union want to affiliate to the newly formed anti-Socialist British Labour Party they will be able to do so, and they can use the general funds of the union to finance anti-socialist, Tory or Liberal candidate. I think this point needs to be enforced. The Bill gives no powers to a trade union to promote Labour candidates under the Labour Party const,itution which cannot be equally used to pr6mote Liberal- Labour or Tory-Labour trade union candi- dates, if a majority of the members of the union should so decide by their votes. The Bill simply gives a trade union the right to use its funds for political purposes to further the interests of workmen ; but it leaves the 'union the fullest liberty to decide which form its action shall take.

The fact I have just pointed out seems to me to remove any grievance which a minority might have on the ground that the trade union was promoting a candidature of a character they could not approve. Every section of a trade union will have as much liberty as any other section to get the candi- dature promoted in the way it would prefer. The Tory trade unionists can get a Tory- Labour candidate if they can command a majority of votes in the union • the Radical trade unionists can get a Radical-Labour candidate if they can command a majority; the Independent Labour Men or Socialists in the trade union can get a candidate of their way of thinking if they can command a majority of votes in the union. So it is fair play for every section, and I fail to see how any minority can have a grievance because they have to submit to a majority after a fair and open contest. If the trade unions with which I am connected were to decide that it is desirable that our craft should be represented in Parliament by a member of the union, and if the decision should be in favour of promoting a candidature in alliance with the the Unionist or Radical party I should regret the choice, but I should not complain. I should set to work 'to make a majority opinion in the union in favour of trade union representation apart from either Liberal or Tory party, which is what the Labour Party stands for. 1111‘. National Union of Teachers have, as a ma ter of fact, done precisely what I have \ just 'magined the jurnalists' !union !might do, hey have used the funds of the union at the last General Election to pay for a Libera candidate, a Unionist candidate, and a La ur candidate. div.head: CHAPTER X.
div.p: CHAPTER X.
MIRIAM TRAFFORD AND AIDZ MORANT AND TRZ ZAVZB-DROPPIR IN THZ BOAT.

Quarry Woods were clothed in green, not a leaf quivered, nor a branch waved, the birds In their flight seemed to hang motionless in the limpid air. There was an absence of life on the river, for which the weather was an- swerable. The low sparkling stream had a glaas-like surface, broken now and then by a sportive fish springing after a foolish fly. For a few weeks the English summer had been tropical in its sultry intensity, the sky dal- sling the eyes, and the sun blistering to the skin. The dreamy languor of the atmoaphere was unbearable, and most ladies were driven to seek the cool shelter of the hpuse-boate and river-side bungalows, while the men had chosen the upper reaches in which to freshen their hot bathes by plunging in the tumbling waters of the weirs. A single skiff passed Marlow Lock, to the surprise of a few loungers, paddled past the church, and then spurted for half a mile, putting plenty of leg- work into each long, dragging stroke, which soon brought the seuller abreast of a grassy lawn, eloping to the river's edge. There he eased off, resting his blades on the surface of the water, folding his muscular arms on the handles of the shafts, displaying to advan- tage his biceps. his depth of chest, and the breadth of his back. This man, who took no heed of the moon-day sun pouring its burning rays on the panama which covered his head, was of prepossessing appearance, and was possessed of a singularly striking physique. His dark brown eves, black hair, close-cut beard, and pointed moustaches, his bronzed complexion and general aspect, gave an on- looker the impression he was an Italian. or Spaniard of the cultured class. His visible Intelligence was remarkable, but - a cynic might take objection to the sinister smile on the thin lips, when regarding the scenery by which he was surrounded. To a judge of phyeiognomy he was unmistakably a man of Intrigue, aggressive in his actions, and cer- tainly unscrupulous in his dealings. While cooling off, his thoughts had slipped back over events in which he had played an exciting part. He bethought him somewhat unwillingly of a foul deed, after accomplish- ing which he had been tricked by the disap- pearance of the pay-master and instigator, than leaving him to bear the brunt of the crime, had it been traced to him. Count Leon Rodrigeux, alias Dorinus, the chauf- feur, was not a person to forgive, there was tio trace of magnanimity in his disposition. Be was the kind of man who would trample on man, woman, or child, in order to attain any end that he might have irk view. He was a man destitute of mercy, flu he was of prin- ciple. Miriam Trafford was the lady he was at that moment about to seek, and she would, In the course of time, regret having made him a pawn in the game that she was play- ing. He threw aside his sweater, wiped- the perspiration from his face, laved his hands in the water, lighted, and pulled industriouitly at a thin South American cigar, while the boat remained stationery, for there was little or no current.
Bringing himself with a jerk from his re- verie, he pulled under a cluster of willows, shipped his sculls, and pillowed his head on the bow cushions.

"Where could elle have flown? Trafford House is apparently deserted. Yes, appa- rently, else why was there a slanting ray of light from that small window, a line of light so thin that few would be smart enough to notice it. But I did. My watchings, how- ever, have ended exactly where they began in nothing. What proof have I wherewith to scare my treacherous female accomplice? I've preserved her note, instructing me to take the poor devil's boots, a lucky hint, for I should never have thought of his name being printed on the loops of his boots. This would have led to an inquiry, the clue would have been conclusive, then would have come expo- sure, in which dear Miriam and I would have been equally involved. Suddenly he looked around. "Saint Paul! That voice!"

He started from his recumbent position so roughly that the skiff was nearly capsized. Fearing that the owner of the voice might de- tect and recognise the smell of the tobacco, he thrust the smoldering cigar in the water, and listened eagerly. Two ladies were in earnest conversation, paring to and fro be- hind the willows where lay the Count, listen- ing eagerly to every syllable. His face wore a look of vindictive triumph, his eyes kept di- lating and closing, like those of a eat. Rub- bing his hands one over the other, he clicked his tongue against his teeth, and laughed Sendiehly to himself.

"I have my fair Miriam at last," he mut- tered between his etrong white teeth, and he stamped his rubber-shod boot on the carpet of the ekiff. He can no beauty in the eum- waer day, he thought only of revenge on the woman who had tried to betray him. The voices row high in dispute, and he lay In the boat, listening. his twitching lips and lashing eyes showing the evil and bate in his heart. "Why am I a prisoner?" demanded a Sweet girlish voice, which had • slight toll* occent.

I will never for- give the insults you have heaped upon ins —ma, your benefactress. Marry or starve,* she concluded, pushing the girl violently away. Aide threw up her arms, her cry of protest reaching the man's ears. "1 am alone, utterly alone," she wailed; than added proudly, "But there is a God above, and Be is with me."
- Miriam shrunk back like a guilty creature, and suffered Aide to leave the garden, and enter the house unmolested. . .

Miriam paced the grassy slope, thinking, "A life, a single life, and—freedom." She had disliked Aide in her childhood, in her girlhood she was jealous of her fair, re- fined beauty, and the love both bore Arabs bad culminated in a hatred, bitter and in. tense. Every nerve and fibre in her superb body was on the rack. She was shaking, for her agony of fear was great. Aide's words might be' words of no import, yet they plainly showed that she susperted ; but how much? She could not answer this important ques- tion. . . . .

"Oh, for certainly! Oh for assured con- viction," she cried aloud in her impatienee. A wicked look passed over her handsome featureg, and a full feeling of defeat took possession of her heart. she grew irritable of the heat, the glaring min, and of her own dis- tracted thoughts. She frowned heavily. and the man tinder the willows saw that there was something threatening in Miriam's as- pect. Gentle as Aide was bv nature, there was that about her which luta made Miriam realise with dread that she had all at onee found her soul, no girl's inner self but the defiant and resolute spirit of a woman. Miriam feared it, and her fear was terrible to behold, terrible in its wickedness. _

Silence, a dead stillnean. The millen quiet of the hitherto sultry day was stirred by tho summer breeze, which ruffled Miriam's hair, waved toe foliage of the trees, and rippled the surface of the slug- gish river.

Between them was a pause long and silent, during which the woman in her alarm gazed at the man, hiding tho workings of her face within the palms of her trembling hands. She shivered, instinctively realising that it was the master of her destiny who then con- fronted her.

He laughed carelessly, if not insolently, their eyes met in a momentary encounter, her face growing hot beneath his triumphant gaze; yet though he smiled, a presentiment of evil stole into his heart. Her consterna- tion subsiding, she sprang to her feet, threw back her head defiantly, all the wild tumult of her paasion breaking into stormy wrath. "Well," said she between her net teeth. "You have come, and what do you want?" "My promised reward," said he promptly. "You have not fulfilled our compact." "How have I failed in it?"

"By not proving that—that---" " That Lawson has hopped the twig." "%an& I do not understand," she rejoined contemptuously. " Well, then, fair princess, to put the slang plainer, the troublesome gentleman may not have quitted this sphere, for the one above or the other below."
"I saw no account in the daily papers of any inquest," she whimpered, her teeth chat- tering as though she had been struck with sudden cold.

"Nor I. The absence of a report has puszled me likewise not a little. Yet when I carried him up the stairs of a villainously dirty house in the vicinity of St. Andrew's. street, and laid him on the landing, he neither .moved .or breathed."
Hash! Hush! You may be heard." She looked through the bushes to be sure of their privacy. Clasping his bare arm, she asked ex- citedly, • • .
"You have that paper?" "Paper !" lie shook his head.
"I have no paper." -- "The torn scrap that I impressed upon you must be got from him." "Now I understand. Well, I marched, but discovered nothing. I suppose I was hurried and nervous."

"Hurried! Nervous! You are a splendid liar, Leon Rodriguez," she exclaimed impa- tiently. "On my honour," be said seriously. " Honour ! Such honour as you possess is but poor thing to swear by or to believe in "

--He grew very pale, his eyes flashing with rage at this open insult. I tell you again I did not find the paper you were so anxious to get hold of. Why don't you trust me?" he asked reproachfully. "I did once, and you abused my confi- dence."
" Clrics entirely to the force of circum- stance,l..
"Our acquaintance wan made at the gam- bling tables of Monte Carlo, recollect," she said significantly. With an informal introduction," he re- torted.

He pondered, took a step forward, and said in low, impressive tones: "Miriam, tell me the motive you had in dooming Lawson to death I" She concealed her features behind her filmy handkerchief. "tell me," he persisted; "toll me in con- fidence. I'll shield you from the results, if you will be frank and honest with me. The motive most indeed have been a powerful one, which could induce • woman Inn urge a man to commit a crime which, if discovered, would certainly lead him to the gallows. You loved Lawson? Don't deny the insinuation, Aerie, for I heard every word of the conversation that passed just now between a young lady and yourself. Yhere's my boat," pushing aside the willow boughs. " And you are a gentleman, Count Rodri- guez," else exclaimed, in • voice of wither- ing _scorn.

"Your sneer is unnecessary, I am not sail- ing under false colours. I am the true, though base, descendant of a noble family," speaking in tones of regret. "Shall we wante hours in reviling each other, when we should be plotting?" he cried impatiently. "I re- quire money, and that must be supplied by you. I am stony-broke." kre laid his band on her shoulder, carpoo- -lln ly, yet with a touch of mastery that it rred her strangely. "Miriam, I am a rank bad hit, and you are unscrupulous, though a divinely beautiful, , oinan.-

"Pah !" throwing off his hand; the days have gone by for aueli silly sentimentality to affect me. To you I surrendered a young girl's greateat treasure, and you treated her yielding lightly. Oh, Leon, how could you be so cruel to me? Scoundrel, bead !" tier

Injured pride, her vanity, and the sense of her wrongn were carrying her beyond the bounds of prudence. She knew that to break the bond that bound them would be fatal to herself, yet she was reckless, and counted not the cost. "Miriam, you are unjust. I was not per- mitted to enter your father's house, and so we had to meet by stealth. I valued Tour confidence, believe me. In your reproaches you have overlooked one thing, which is, that I did lore you." "And I you, then," she cried passionately. "Your presence used to fill me with unutter- able bliss, unscrupulous though I was. It was my training amidst a Court of cunning intrigue and wicked diplomacy that has made me what I am. None ean undo the training of years. You had it in your power to teach me better things had you chosen to do it. You might have taught me goodness. Oh, that I could recall the years. and be a child again- But it is impossible. Measured by the world's standard, I am a woman to be- ware of—a suspect. I use both you and my- self as we are. "Miriam. have von Aceated me Miele?" he

cried. •• 1 say no. hear me to the ena. t ou, for some purpose which you have not yet di- vulged. persuaded me to knock a poor devil, who had escaped your clutches. op the head. The deed done, and the man .11.1 y disposed of, you disappeared. For twelve months I have never ceased my search for you; to meet you has been the sole object ot my lite. Just its my means were exhausted, chance brought me to your door, and here I intend to_ remain." . . . . . . .

Miriam gave a short, hysterical laugh. "There are instances," be went on in the same strain, "rare, perhaps, yet true, when a man does not value a woman to the full till he believes that he has lost her," sigh.
intiriam threw up her chin, a mingled look of distrust and pleasure flitting across her handsome tare. "Inconstancy is inherited, not_rultivated." she said sagely.
His sarcastic smile brought the blood to her cheeks, a blush of shame and humilia- Von." . . .

• "You made me vow to be true. I wee true. Were you true to me?, be demanded severely. "No, no, false." "In thought only. Not being your wife, I deny your right to question me.", "In less than three moons you shall be the Countess Rodrigues. Remember we are partners in crime." She shrank before the steady light in his eyes; those eyes which bad always influ- enced her so strongly that even now .be wavered and faltered. There was a repres- slon in his voice that was to her a repression and an earnestness such as she had never heard before. But could she believe again his protestations of loyalty? Could she capi- tulate to him and resign her freedom? Could she endure for the remainder of her life to know no other will but his? Could she ever be to him a submissive wife? To obey, where she once had ruled/ Iler very soul rose up at the idea, and cried out a denial. The man's assured air of ownership chafed her proud and exacting nature, and ehe resolved that there should be no compromise ..etween them.

"I have no palace, nor lands, nor fortune, only a title to lay at the feet of my prin. ten," he went on. "A tarnished title," she retorted viciously. "Yes, stained with blood,' he interjected with a certain ring in his voice which forced her to recoil and droop her bold and fiery eyes. "I am penniless; you, my divinity. are wealthy. An excellent combination, riches and poverty. Come," said he coaxingly, "show some confidence in the man who loves you. No, don't sneer, I repeat, who loves you spite of all your faults, your avarice, your cunning, and your heartless deception. You see, cher* I am not ignorant of your least charnxlag self. Totting up our failings, they corns to this, we are a couple of mercenary, milieu creatures, obtaining the pleasures of life at the cost of those unfortunate enough to come between us and our gratifica- tions. We are equally matched; therefore, I offer you my name with my eyes open. Miriam, you might as well try to stop a mad horse in its flight as to turn me from the coin.. I have laid down for us to follow. My wife shall not be censured by man or woman. Be sure I will protect you. - She evaded a direct or immediate reply. Flinging her fan on the gram, she turned away impatiently and walked further into the shrubbery, while he stood watching her. At present he was on the horns of a dilemma, for his pockets were empty, he was hope- lessly involved in debt, los credit was nil, and to add to these embarrassmentn there was the constant dread of being involved in a murder e•Se.
"By-the-bye, are you the Miss Guthrie the lock-keeper described to me? He went into raptures over your beauty, and your kindness to the poor. An you Miss Guthrie here, or Miss Trafford?"

She heettated sullenly, then bowed her bead, drumming the bark of a tree with her Roger tips, that she might hide the trembling of her limbs, for, in truth, she was rapidly melting towards the man to whom she had given once herself, and afterwards bad no fiercely hated. Moreover, she realised that he was a master it would be dangerous to of- fend.
"You look Pale, Miriam," said he, affect- ing a concern which most assuredly he did not feel. "The excessive heat," she murmured . .

faintly. "Or the man. Which?" She was rebellious again. She could not endore his thrust'. Her upper lip curved, her bosom heaved, her tongue was eager to pour ' the fire of her wrath upon his head. To her annoyance, he leisurely lighted a cigar, and sat down on the turf. Ile allowed an amosed chuckle to escape him, and compelled Miriam to sit by his side. Imprisoning her waist, he said: "We are secluded from the eves of scandalmongers. My divine tigress, don't you think we ellen make a splendid pair?" Then, all at once, hie manner changing, he discarded his cyni- cism. and spoke firmly, but respectfully and "Beloved, listen to me:, he began. She moved restlessly, and he re- strained her attempt to rise. "Sit still," he said sternly. "You are mine by right, if not yet by the rites of the Church. Your fancy during my absence strayed for a little while Michsel Lawson, that young man of much Mystery. I forgive and forget what I regard as en error of judgment on your part. It shall be referred to no more. We now stand face to face with the consciousness, of our crime, our sin; call the affair by any .name you please. For either of us to indulge in sentimental retrospection is a waste of men- tol energy." "You have the power in your hands. I am but a puppet dancing this way and that, ac- cording as you choose to poll the stringy." Her voice sank, her haughty pride seemed to have left her. Leaning her cheek upon his shoulder, she murmured: "My reputation and life are in your keeping." "Both are safe," he rejoined, ix the same low tone. "You are a bad man; I am no better. We are aware of our faults. You wieh me to be your wife?" There was a thigh on her cheeks. a brilliancy in her lovely eyes that ealxlued him. .
" I do," he said earnestly. "I will connent upon certain conditions."

"And they are " "Heck and find the other half of this chart, whirl, is a guide, I am convinced, to my father's missing gold." "The other half," said he, studying the piece of torn paper. "How did you become possessed of this?" he asked in a forbidding tone. "It was found in my father's clenched fin. ger." She glanced fearfully around. The man.e arm relaxed its hold on her waist. "Is the Khan dead" he said bluntly. The woman's heart leapt, and sho grew ghastly pale. "Why ask such an absurd ques- tion?" She was almost unconscious, and leaned heavily against his shoulder. "To discover you, I have watched Trafford Armee, and I noticed the other night that faint light was visible, shining from • small grated window at the top of the house. I on several occasions from where I stood a shadow on the blind. If the house is empty, who was in that room?" Miriam glanced at him keenly, but no rapidly that the movement of her eyes was unnoticeable. "There is a caretaker, of course," she said. "A caretaker!" he repeated. "Of course. One would not leave such a house as that without a watchman," she re- plied. "Shall we proceed with the business in hand?" He assented thoughtfully. "And the con. ditions?" he asked. "Recover my diamond necklace, which was stolen by a burglar. Here is a written description of it." "Have you notified the police of the lose?" "No, nor do I intend to do an. You understand I Adieu." And he paddled quietly away along the shore. Schooling her featuren to a statu- esque calm, elm hastened to meet an elderly Frenchman, who, boat-hook in hand, stepped jauntily from the dingey to the lawn. Flourishing his straw hat, he bowed elabo- rately, saying, "Gallant, charming lady, do I find you well?" "Good morning, Monsieur Simard. Who is the gentleman in the boat?" "Mademoiselle, permit me to have the dis- tinguished honour of introducing to you my esteemed preserver and friend, Mr. Alco Elandford." . .

The Queen's Canopy.—The "canopy drichorses" at the Coronation of King Edward and Queen Alexandre, were the Duchess of Montrose, the Duchess of Suther- land, the Duchess of Portlind, and the Duchess of Marlborough. The Brat three mentioned been again been selected to carry the Queen's canopy at the Coronation next June, the fourth being the Duchess of Hamilton, the cite of the premier Scottish duke. It was thought that the Duchess of Westminster would be one of the chosen quartette, but the duchesses who are eligible as canopy-holders, are very limited in number as they have to be of even height, and more than commonly tall, especially on this occasion as the Queen herself is dowered with a goodly number of inch.. The suggestion that the four ducheasess should be chimen to represent England, Scotland, Ireland, and Wale., was found to be Impracticable. Scotland, at any rate, has no reason to complain of her share of this ooveted office at the Coronation, for although the Duchess of Hamilton is an Englishwoman, three of the four canopy-holders are the wive. of Scottish duke& _ _

--The London Season.—There have been three new ducheeses since the Iset Coronation, namely, the Ditches. of Devonshire, the Duehese of ttoxbuighe,and the Duchess of Rutland. The first named, it is said, will revive the Derby night dinner, and dance, at Devonshire Howe, which was one of tho chief social : events of the London season, in King Edward's time. King Edward used to entertain the members of the , Jockey Club at Buckingham Palace, going on rifler words Ito the hall at Devonshire Doom After the death of the late Duke of Devonshire, Lord and Lady Ferguhe r gave the Derby night dinner and dance at their house 'in Grosvenor square. Lord arid Lady loarguhar have long been among tbe favoured hosts of Royalty, and the first dinner party attended by the King and Qimen niece May, woe given at their house last week. In thus : dining privately with personal friends, the King and : Queen are following a cuatorn which King Edward and Queen Alexandra extended to numerous London hosts and hostesses. Women in Place of Men-Servants—. Jeanine " is gradually disappearing like the British waiter, and in wealthy (miller; chief parlourmaide In smart liveries are taking the place of the butler and footman. They oan do all the men servants do, are more useful about the house in other ways, and are lessexpeneive At the same time this tendency will help to rase the wages of women servants generally, which is not good news for the middle-class families, who do not keep men- aaaaa nts. As for the ordinary British waiter, where he survives the competition of the foreigner, he is being ousted from his office by the weitress, who, in ever- increasing numbers, is taking his place. The Brearbßeforrn Movement —The making of home. made bread, like the making of home-brewed beer, ranks among the lost domestic arts in this country. (Sissies' maintained that no maid of whatsoever rank should be allowed to wed unless she" could make e perfect loaf of bread." That, however, mean. a lot of trouble, and seeing that we are entirely in the hands of the bakers, there is much to be said for the contention that a nutritive standard of bread should he enforced by legislation, in the same way that there is a legal atandard of quality for milk and butter. The "bread reform "innermost bay extended very widely, bet it in skid that much of what is sold as "standerd "bread, is not what it pretends to be, that is bread made from goer containing the full nutritive value of the wheet berry. Seeing that this is a matter intimately con- nected with the physical sell.being of the nation, and especially the younger population, there is clearly need for legislative action to ensure for the public a supply of good wholesome nourishing breed. Dietary Prejudices.—We have our International prejudices about bread as well as other articles of food. It hes been said that the Nepoleonio wars really had their origin in our contempt for • nation that ate frogs and mails, and within the lest year or no, we have bean invited to commiserate with the Germane on their hard lot in having to eat black bread, horse•flesh and dog-most. Then the rabbit is popular in France and appreciated—if a little common—in this country, but in Germany it is on a lower level than the dog, and scarcely better than vermin. Rye, i,f which German bread is largely .niposed is now but little used for bread-making in this country, although it greatly helps to keep the loaf moiet and fresh. Those who bane travelled on the Continent ere mostly of *pinion that, for taste, there is no bread to equal that one gets in Penn, but many connoissenres declare that the best bread in Europe is to be found In Russia. div.head: LIBERAL ACTIVITY. SUCCESSFUL MEETINGS IN THE WARDS
div.p: LIBERAL ACTIVITY. SUCCESSFUL MEETINGS IN THE WARDS
Speeches by Mr H. New.

It wan A happy idea on the part of the organisers of the Liberal Party in Warrington, when it was mug- ' gested that the committees of each ward in the ;borough should meet once month, so as to au•dain the interest in the progressive cause and also to diacuas various phases of pditics. On Saturday evening last the first of these meetings took place at the Liberal Club in connection with liewsey Ward, the special feature if the evening being an address by Mr. Harry New. Mr. Joseph )wen pre- sided over a good attendance, which included Councillor+ Wilkinson, Skelland and Dickenson, Messrs. Peter Peacock, If. New, E. A. Sanders, and P. lielseey. Various suggestions were made as to the carrying on of propaganda work. Afterwards Mr. New delivered a lecture on 'The Parliament Bill." Ile dee!, with his subject in a lucid manner pointing out souse of the more preminent Pills which had either been thrown out or mutilated by the House of Lords. The statement that it was high time that the House ti lords had their powers clipped was received with enthusiasm by those present. The very fact of the Liberal party hang elected by such a magnificent majority as they were in Ilan; ought to have had the acknowledgement of the II tote of Lords bur they took no notice of that circumstance. The members of the Liberal patty in the t iovernment were men who had been in touch with the voters all their lire. and their time had been given in eerving the cause of the people and it was far from just that they should be flouted by a number of Peers, who were out of touch with the people's needs and desires and woe not qualified to judge what was beet for the majority. (Applause,. The diemisaion was taken part in by Menses. W. Patrick, 11. Wright, R. Jones, P. Peacock and P. Delaney.
Howley Ward. MIL NEW AND INCOME AND VALUE.

A meeting of the Howley Ward Executive end General Committee, under the new organization, was held at the Liberal Club. on Wedneaday evening. Prior to the I;eneral Committee meeting a meeting of the Executive was held. A diactissi,m took Ow, on the affairs of the ward generally, and various sogges• tines were made by the members, and recotornerida- time were taken for consideration by the General !Committee.

A (tenet-al Committee meeting was afterwards held at which Mr. W. Clegg presided over, large atten- dance of about forty members. Amongst that.. present were Messrs. M. I.lewelyn (nice-chairman), W. Voile and Ilamblett (honwecretaries), ll. New lagent).and E. Sanders (aaaistant agent). The ininwee of the last meeting having been read and formally adopted. The Chairman, in a few remarka, reminded the members that that meeting was the first oft series of monthly meetings under the new organisation. It was hoped, he said. that much good work would be accomplished on behalf of the working classes of the borough. Mr. New, in an interesting addre.s on ' Income and value." an relating to land, pave several interesting instances of how land increased in value under private ownership as years went on. In opening his address he said it was hit privilege to explain to them the meaning of income and value and its relationship Ii the workers of this country. Mr. New ehowed how laud, when in the hands of private owners, increased enormously in value. He gave one sttiking example. In 1896 Mr. E. T. Hooley, the great financier, bought the Lafford Park Mats for £300,1100. Twelve month, later, in 1c:17, he sold the estate to the Trafford Park Estate Co. for 0901.(kab making a profit of .C. 10,000 on the transaction. Another striking example the spesker gave wee one in which a man, twenty years ego, had land worth 5.:).01.0) per acre. The owner refused to sell, saying he could wait. Five years ago the man died and the land fetched 015.001) an acre, or !15,000 for three acres. On that same piece of land, Mr. New added, there were now rows of Hats and ahope with a rental of Its each. The Hats had only four rooms but they were not suitable for the working classes. At the clots, of the address, questions were asked. and a discuesion took place, taken part in by the Chairman, Mr. Llewellyn and Slr. Bissell. The Chairman and lecturer sere heartily thanked at the : close.

you kindly allow me the courtesy of your columns to bring before the notice of your mita:, readers an anomaly practised by the Warrington Corporation, and its effect upon the general welfare of the community. more especi- ally from the standpoint of the public health? For many years there have not been wanting signs that the authorities have become interested in questions of hygiene and sanitation, and, indeed, these signs apparently go b• prove that they are of opinion that money spent upon WI. i moving the conditions under Which the majority of our perle.live money well spent..

Th. 'Education Conintitiee is an admirable example of this satisfactory state of affairs: The members seem to vie with each other as to the provision of the best and healthiest sites for new schools, whilst those already erected are models of their kind. These gentlemen seem to be over-' zealous for the provision of healthy epaces, for Alderman Bennett would have purchased the Orford.roed site last week for a recreation ground. This idea would, of course, have been an excellent ogre hail there been any real dangers of the vicinity becoming a desert of bricks and chimney its during the next few generations. Again, occasionally we hear murmuring, from the Parks nn 1 Baths Committee of their Intel, lions to make open.air ixatlis to encourage clean- This, again, is excellent, but the curious anomaly of wide'. I write is that these gentlemen are overlooking the cheapest and most suitable means likely to bring about the conditions required; cheapest because it is without cost to the Corporation, and lIIOSt is iteble because the means would lie to every Titan's hands. I mean the erection of baths in workmen's dwellings. One. everywhere and always. is hearing and answering the query, " Why don't the builders put baths in every house?" Here is the reply: The cost of a modern bath, including all fittings, is approximately £l2. The Corporation impiriAli no additional water rate if n tap is tined Mel' the bath. In pril, tii ;Eitioup himself for the pre- !Military outlay and' the extra rate charges the rent nutst be raised by is. per week. This ranges the assessment of It tii leap up 21 /os., and the owner tlf the property loses the com- position. Now mark the difference.

..... The net rates payable for a three-roomed house. with a bath, at Ers. per week, are £4 4s. lid.' The net rates for a similar house, without a bath, at is. per work. are £2 se. 4r1., eo that of the addi- tional Is. per week of increased rent the Corpora- trm commandeers £1 Igs. Td. per year. Yet note the glaring inconsistent-y. If a bath be fixed without a tap above it.. in mar bathe to your heart's content without charge: but if you adopt the sensible plan of placing the tap over the bath yotl are twittered in On increased rate of £1 Igs. Til. Few working men can afford to pay this Is. per week as extra rent for the luxury of a both in the house; and there is little inducement for the buildets to tempt hint to do no for the turn of 12s. 54, yearly—his altars of the increase for renewal and profit. If the Corporation are really desirous of pro. sorting cleanliness, if they no sincerely in earnest in thi, declared warfare against the evils of insanitation and disease, they will remove this ridiculous imposition front all boluses of a less ratable value of £lO or 6s. per week. Is there no member of the Council—now that the anomaly has been exposed—who will move in the interests of the working class, and who will work without ceasing, for the removal of these MINA impediments to the progress of sanitation and the health of our own I—Yours, ele, GEORGE SMITH. The Limes, Orton', Warrington, March 6.

Sir,—There ie no need to impute ineincerity to your correspondent.. the Rev. Walter Seed, by the affirniaticn that his strictures on Christian Science are the outcome of miniature judgment. Indeed, it is obvious that he has given exnreeeirdt only to what he honestly believes :tie impressions of the subject to be, and If it is difficult to are his wholesale condenmation as merely a "passing , reference.' or to reconcile the statement that it was made "thoughtfully and with full grounds after serious at tidy " with the disclaimer of the right to he regarded so an authority on the snit ject, V is, at any rate, easy to commend the limb avowal that any light from. And herein lies the very crux of the matter. Herein lies the very secret of Christianity. Were that so,, as one know, ii is not claimed to be, then the Minene of that true light wookL be his, and there would be no new light to welcor,e. What test, then, are we to employ? As to,, exponent of eternal truth, as the deliverer of Me good tidings which should earn for him the title of the Saviour of mankind, Jesus could not ban meant, when he 1.11141 that those who believed en Him should do the works he did, that his words were to he restricted to the few fishermen who beard them. Mites advanced as an excuse for neglecting to insist that the signs to look for in determining the due of a teaching should be those signs . whim n in His last words on earth Jesus said , ,ehould " follow them that believe." ' Now Chrietian Science teaches that this may all lie summed up in one sentence, "Christianity is demonstrable truth." Where would all the sects, anti schient, and the strife and jealousy they etand for, he if all had to prove the truth of their teaching? As there is but one truth, so there could be but one creed, the creed of Christ. And Christian Science invites this lest to be applied to it, and it offers an alninet unending array of instances of sin giving place to goodness, nr sick ness, sorrow, and selfishness giving place to health and peace and love. which beyond all donht proves that the gospel it preaches is not after man. • " . .

Mr critic takes exception to the statement that ftOd never made man capable of sin as opposed to the Bible promise that we should be saved (rom our sins. Every ray of "true light" that Nunes to our consciousness ensue, in destruction ,of darkness. And as this light can but he know- ledge of the truth, every glimpse of it must come to us in destruction of a false belief. The sink.er sins because of his false belief that he sill enjoy or get some good out of it. The sick su..l sorrowful are so because of the world's belief in the power and reality of evil, not because they are ordained of God. Jesus said the most im, port•nt commandment for us to keep was the command to ascribe all power to God. good. The rust conspiracy of the hurrian mind to disobey 'thie constitutes the seeming reality of evil. To crush that conspiracy is the mission of Chris, tiaLity, and to disclose to man his real nature as the first page of the Bible declares Him to us, male in the image and likeness of God. is its redemptive function. And eo when one awakes to the realisation that the real man never sins, but that the sinner is the false human coneeot of man as a mortal material being apart from God. it is seen that the knowledge of God, or Truth. does save from such a concept, and so froni sin. As evil grows less and less real with the developing understanding of the onmi presence and omnipotence of God. an do we in a corresponding degree gradually cease to manifest it. This is not to assume that those who cannot " let that mind be in them which was aleo in, Christ Jesus" are "mentally incanable." but it is to.declare that the all.ness of God is. through Christian Science, filling more and .more the coneciousnese of men to the exclusion of error. and that it will continue an to do until the earth is full of the knowledge of the Lord as the waters ,cover the sea —Yours, Yours' li;;ILIAM J. div.head: RECTOR AND ROME. The Rector Replies to Father Whittle.
div.p: THE RECTOR AND ROME. The Rector Replies to Father Whittle.
Sir,—ln the intereits of truth. and for the information of all who would he true Catholics it is necessary to reply to the miwetatements of Father Whittle.

1. The Catholic Church has always conceded, not to the Bishop, but to the Church, of Rome, for various reasons a Primacy of Honour and Love, but Supremacy—never. That this Primacy of the Church of Rome was one ~f Honour and Love only we clearly infer from the letter of Clement, the third Bishop of Rome, to the Coritithiana,and are distinctly told so by Ignatius, the second Bishop of Antioch, in his letter to the Romans. There he expressly calls it • " Presidency of Love." Tlvre were originally five Patriarchates and the order of their foundation was as follower Antioch, Rome, Alexandria.Constantinople,.fornsalem. Later on because of the importance of some of the localities, the order was changed and liscamo this Rome, Conatantinople,Alexandria,Antioch, Jernsalem,anil so It has remained ever since. Four of these Patriarchates were in the East alld but one in the West, all on A . perfectly equal footing; but inasmuch as the Western one had its seat in Imperial Rome, the great capital of the world, the false notion grew up and gradually gained ground, furthered by the departure of the Emperors ~o. 300 to Constantinople. that it was the only one. and no was laid the foundation for that nionatrona perversion of truth that the Bishop of Rome was the only real Pattiatch and Head of the Church upon earth. *2. The Eastern Church rightly regards God the Father an the sole Fount of Deity. She does not deny that the Buy Spirit proceeds from the Father by the Son, but she considers that whnt im called the Double Procession is open to misconstruction, and so she is opposed to the " Filiorine." But what she chiefly and rightly objects to is that the Church of Rome should, on her own authority alone, and contrary to the decrees of the two great Councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon in 431 and 431, have added this article to. the Faitlh rn she did in the year .180, and no broiled about the great schism of the East and West in 1051. And it is worth while noting that so late as the year SOO, Pope Leo 111, declined to sanction the interpola- tion. It would almcst seem from Father Whittle's word. that he connidem the Athanosian Creed to be , the work of St. Athattaius He should know that it was not composed-until 511 years after his death arid is of Western not Eastern origin. 3. if Father Whittle will read his Bible he trill find that we are not told what words our Lord used in Consecrating the Holy Eucharist. The Sacred Narratives simply say "lie blessed " and "lie gave thanks " ; and if he will study the ancient Liturgies he will find that the Church not knowing what words He used, foes thousand years taught that the Conae- cration was effected by the power of God after the Invocation of the Holy Spirit, as the Eastern Church still teaches. And this is a use which we are thankful to say the Churches of England, Scotland and Arneyica have followed. About a thousand years ago or more the Church of Rome substituted what is simply the Recital of our Lord's Words and Acts. for the Invocation and made the Change dependent upon the utterance by the PH« at of the woris "Thin is My Body," "This is 31y Blood " which were the words of Communion, not of Consecration. . .

4. And not., what is the nature of the Change ? It in here that we shall find the most rocothulic teaching of Rome. I will defy Father Whittle to quote any Father down to the Council of Chalcedon in -151 who believed that after Consecration the elements ceased to exist in their own proper nature ; and in confirmation of this I will give him the words of fielasins. a great Bishop of Rome who lived 50 years later about A.l) 500. "The elements abide in their own proper nature." What will Father Whittle say to this, and how will he reconcile it with modern Roman teaching ? Further, I will challenge Father Whittle to mune any Gteek Father who used the word " Slermisiosis " or any Latin scholar who notes the word " Transubstantiation " before the eleventh century, though I admit that the false doctrine eignified be this some was first taught tflvi years earlier by Paschasius Radbert. And if neither he nor anyone else can accept my challenge one can only marvel at the folly of the Church of Route which in . the lice of the clear testimony of the Fathers art to the nature of the Sacrament, and in opposition to the direct statement of one of their own wrest Popes, and finally in contradiction of the express words of St. l'aul in I Coo. xi. 214, end it would seem of our Lord i Himself in St. Matt. xxvi. t!ft. and St. Mark xiv, Minister, on her people the groundleee merli,eval doctrine of Transubatantiation. The Fathers never used the word " Metousiosis," which I the equivalent oh " Transubstantiation," and implies the change of the whole auhstance. It is the one word which they ever avoided, though they used many similar words which all denote a change, a change such as all true Catholics believe in. vic., a Sacramental change, a change that is, by way of addition. Before Consecra- tion, simply Bread and Wine, after, still Bread and Wine, but also The Body and Blood of Christ Out- wardly Bread and Wine, Inwardly The Body and Blood of Chriat. 'This i. the Catholic doctrine of the Real Presence. Junta word in ccticlasion as to our Orders. The Eastern Church is orthodox and conservative. She regm chi Rome as heretical and achismstic and in her isolation and ignorance of Western affairs and modern occurrences has looked upon the Church of England until lately as one of the various Religious Bodies ' which separated from the Church of Rome in the 114th, century ; but she is beginning to know bettiiir. She is now interested in our history She is studying our Orders and we believe that in God's good time, if we are only faithful to the Doctrine and Practice of the Primitive and Catholic Church, an acknowledgement will come and a Reunion take place for which every : true Catholic must long and every true Catholic reasele,d, pray. At present and an long as the Church cf Rome persists in her errors, mnon with her is, sad to say, impossible.—Youra, Ac., FREDERIC W. WILLIS, The Rectory, Warrington.

One of these points ties" For nearly 1,000 years the whole Church believed that the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ in the Holy Communion depended upon the Invoca- tion of the Holy Spirit. but about 1,10(X) years after Christ the Church of Rome took it upon herself to substitute the words of Institution 'Tints is My Body.' 'This is My Blood 'for the Invocation of the Holy Spirit."
